title: Allegheny County is reassessing every property – here’s how your tax bill is calculated now
paragraphs: Allegheny County will undergo a countywide reassessment of every property it taxes for the first time since 2012. A county judge ordered the reassessment in August 2026, requiring the work to begin by July 1, 2027, and finish within five years.

The goal is to bring property values in line with today’s market. That could shift the tax burden among property owners across the county. State anti-windfall rules may require local governments to lower their tax rates after a reassessment to ensure they balance and equalize the tax reassessments. Individual bills may go up or down.

For many homeowners, property taxes are confusing. Terms such as assessment, millage rate and school district tax come up often, but taxpayers may not know what they mean or how each one affects their annual tax bill.
In Pittsburgh, property taxes pay for schools, parks, libraries, public safety and other local services.
I research and teach government finance at Penn State Harrisburg, including a course on state and local taxation. Here’s a plain-language guide to how Pittsburgh’s property taxes work.
The first concept is the property assessment. Allegheny County’s Office of Property Assessments gives every property an assessed value. That value is the basis for calculating property taxes.

An assessed value isn’t necessarily what a home would sell for today. Some places, such as Philadelphia, assess property at full market value. Other jurisdictions assess property at a set percentage of market value. In Cook County, Illinois, which includes Chicago, homes are assessed at 10% of their market value. That doesn’t mean Chicago-area homeowners pay less. When assessments are a smaller share of market value, tax rates are set higher to raise the same amount of money. Allegheny County assesses at full value, but it uses what properties were worth in 2012. The court-ordered reassessment is meant to close the gap between those 2012 values and today’s market.

Allegheny County’s 14-year gap would be unusual almost anywhere else. Pennsylvania is the only state that doesn’t require counties to reassess on a regular schedule, while most states do so at least every six years. Within Pennsylvania, though, Allegheny is far from the worst: Butler County hasn’t reassessed since 1969.
Homeowners can look up their assessment on the county’s real estate portal.

Once a property has an assessed value, each local government applies a millage rate to figure out the tax owed. One mill equals $1 of tax for every $1,000 of assessed value. A home assessed at $100,000 has 100 units of $1,000 in value.
Pittsburgh property owners pay property taxes to three government entities: Allegheny County, the City of Pittsburgh and Pittsburgh Public Schools. Each one sets its own millage rate.

For 2026, the city’s general rate is 9.67 mills. The city also charges 0.5 mill for parks and 0.25 mill for libraries. Pittsburgh Public Schools charges 10.457 mills, and Allegheny County charges 6.43 mills.
Together, those rates add up to 27.307 mills. For a city home assessed at $100,000, that comes to about $2,731 a year before any exemptions or discounts.

The county’s property tax worksheet and the county treasurer’s millage rate page list current rates. These rates are set each year, and all of them will be cut when reassessed values take effect, since the law requires rates to drop as total values rise.

School taxes are often the largest share of a homeowner’s property tax bill. In Pennsylvania, property taxes are a major source of revenue for public schools. They help fund salaries for teachers, updates and maintainance for buildings, transportation, and technology and educational programs.

School tax rates vary widely across Allegheny County. Pittsburgh Public Schools charges 10.457 mills, well below the suburban districts around it. North Allegheny, one of the lowest-taxing suburban districts, charges about 20.4 mills for the 2026-27 school year. Two of the highest are Mt. Lebanon at about 32 mills and Penn Hills at about 32.6 mills. The county treasurer publishes a full list of school district rates.
Some homeowners qualify for programs that lower their tax bills.

The Allegheny County Homestead exemption, known as Act 50, cuts $18,000 from the assessed value of a qualified, owner-occupied, primary residence property’s county taxes. There’s no income limit: Any homeowner who lives in the property as their primary residence qualifies. A home assessed at $100,000 is taxed on just $82,000, which saves about $116 a year. Enrolling in Act 50 also automatically applies Pittsburgh’s $15,000 exemption, which covers the parks and library levies, and a larger Pittsburgh Public Schools exemption that is set each year. Applications for this exemption are due March 1 and need to be filed only once.

The senior citizen tax relief program, known as Act 77, takes another 30% off county taxes for homeowners who are at least 60, have household incomes of $30,000 or less and have owned and lived in their home for at least 10 years. For a qualifying senior with that $100,000 home, the county bill would drop from about $527 to about $369.

Homeowners who believe their assessment is too high can appeal their assessment to the county’s Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review. Filing is free; appeals can be submitted online, by email or in person.

Appeals are filed the year before the tax year they affect. The appeal window for 2027 bills closed Sept. 1, 2026. The next window, for 2028 bills, is expected to run from July 1 to Sept. 1, 2027, around the time the reassessment is set to begin.

At an appeal hearing, homeowners can argue their property’s value using either 2012 prices or today’s market. Recent sales of similar homes nearby can help show whether an assessment is out of line. The board can lower the assessment, leave it as is or raise it.

Pittsburgh property taxes come down to two elements: the property’s assessed value and the millage rates set by the county, the city and the school district. Understanding how these elements work together can help homeowners read and comprehend their tax bills and better plan for one of the biggest ongoing costs of owning a home, next to the mortgage payment.

That understanding will matter more as the reassessment gets underway. When new values take effect, some homeowners will see their share of the tax burden rise and others will see it fall. The direction depends on how their property’s value has changed compared with changes of other similar properties since 2012.

title: From 18th-century false ballots to the second JFK and double Dan Sullivans, a brief history of spoiler candidates and the unsuccessful legal challenges to them
paragraphs: Less than a week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that people with links to Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola’s U.S. Senate campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee had recruited a candidate to the race whose name is nearly identical to that of the incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, whom Peltola was challenging. The plan aimed to siphon votes from the incumbent senator and help Peltola win, according to the reporting.

The story has driven calls for prosecutions, lawsuits and state action. But as a political scientist who studies election law, I can say that the spoiler candidate is one of the oldest tricks in the American campaign toolbox, and the law has rarely touched it.
For most of the 1800s, American elections were conducted with ballots designed and printed by the parties. There were no official ballots printed by the state.

In those days, the addition of a rival name to a party ballot by an insidious printer could swing countless votes to the opposing party. The tactic was well known, and voters were often warned to look out for the “Spurious Ticket.”
By the 1890s, the government-printed ballot had gained widespread adoption and ended the practice of counterfeit tickets. But that would not be enough to deter those who wanted to deceive voters.
As observers in Alaska have noted, recruiting candidates with similar or identical names is not a new move.

In John F. Kennedy’s first congressional primary, his opponent was a city councilor named Joseph Russo. An aide to Kennedy reportedly paid a janitor with the same name to enter the race. The real Russo complained, but in the end, Kennedy took more votes in the 1946 race than the Russos combined.

Eight years later, the name Kennedy worked the other way, when a Gillette stockroom supervisor named John Francis Kennedy, no relation, was elected as a Democrat to the position of treasurer and receiver-general of Massachusetts, owing in large part to the familiarity of his name. Names can move votes, so namesakes can be worth recruiting.
Some spoiler candidates are not necessarily meant to win votes. Sometimes they are there to amplify a message.

In 1978, Republican Carroll Campbell was running for an open House seat in upstate South Carolina. His opponent was Max Heller, the mayor of Greenville and a Jewish refugee from Nazi-occupied Austria.

Days before the election, Don Sprouse, an independent running for office for the first time, held a press conference and declared that Heller was unfit for office as he had “not made clear to the voters he is not a Christian” and was “not as qualified to represent the Christian people.”

Although Campbell condemned the remarks and Sprouse received only 1,693 votes, Heller lost the race. The allegations, still unproven, of Sprouse being a “stalking-horse” for Campbell only surfaced years later, but they continued to dog Campbell when he ran for governor in 1986.
Sprouse wasn’t going to spoil the election with the votes he could win, but he could be a spoiler with his message, an antisemitic appeal that Campbell would not make directly.
A different type of ballot shenanigan skips the recruitment and simply puts candidates on the ballot.

This was the case in 2010 when two Oakland County, Michigan, Democratic officials put candidates on the ballot under the Tea Party label in three races. The candidates didn’t even know they were running.
In this case, the law did come back to bite. The county party chair and operations director were charged with perjury and forgery, but the crime was forging signatures, not their strategy.

Some state election codes specifically discuss false declarations or forged election paperwork, but many don’t contemplate this type of scheme. Forgery and perjury, however, are illegal across the country, and it’s almost impossible to put an unwitting person on the ballot without one or the other.

In Alaska, this tactic can be used cheaply. There is no petition requirement to get on the ballot, just a $100 fee. Moreover, the parties can’t vet candidates in the primary. The state’s unique top-four primary system lets candidates choose their own party label.
The saga of Daniel J. Sullivan, the schoolteacher known as “Petersburg Sullivan” because of where he lives, and Sen. Dan S. Sullivan goes back longer than recent revelations.

Petersburg Sullivan filed to run as a Republican in the Senate race just three days before the deadline; state officials tried to bar him from the ballot. In June a judge said there was nothing in Alaska law to prevent him from appearing on the ballot, and the state Supreme Court subsequently agreed.

Since he couldn’t be removed, the state Division of Elections took unusual steps on their ballot design to help distinguish the two candidates. They listed Sen. Dan S. Sullivan as a Republican, marking him as the incumbent, and left Daniel J. Sullivan without a party designation. This had not been done for previous incumbents in at least a decade.

Assuming there is no forgery of documents with an unwitting and unwilling spoiler candidate, there is little the law can do. History shows us that the real legal exposure in these cases usually lies where it most often does in politics: money.

In a 2020 Miami, Florida, race, a former state senator turned political operative was convicted of three felonies related to efforts to recruit and pay a decoy candidate with the same surname as the Democratic incumbent. In another Florida case, a local Republican Party chair was convicted in connection with a scheme to plant a progressive alternative to siphon votes from the Democratic candidate. In both cases the prosecutions focused on campaign finance crimes, not simply on putting the spoilers on the ballot.

The state of Washington is an outlier, where it is a felony to run under a rival’s surname if the intent is to confuse voters. In 2024, two Bob Fergusons were recruited by conservative activist Glen Morgan to run for governor against state Attorney General Bob Ferguson. Both opted to drop out of their race under threat of prosecution.

title: Zombies are real – just ask the parasites taking over the bodies and brains of insects and rodents, leading them to their doom
paragraphs: Zombies have taken many forms in popular culture. In Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” music video, corpses climb out of their graves and perform an impressively coordinated dance. In HBO’s “The Last of Us,” a fungus infects humans, takes over their bodies and turns them into hosts that help spread the infection. Even Plankton has tried his hand at taking control of another organism in “SpongeBob SquarePants.”

These examples are fictional, but they all play with the same unsettling idea: Can one organism take control of another, even after they’re dead? In nature, the answer is not quite as dramatic, but some parasites and fungi come surprisingly close.

I spend much of my time as a biomedical engineer and synthetic biologist thinking about how biological systems sense signals, process information and change their behavior. That is part of what makes the idea of one organism taking control of another so fascinating to me.

Some parasites and fungi can alter the behavior of a living host in ways that benefit the parasite. They do not bring the dead back to life. Instead, they interfere with biological systems that control movement, motivation and decision-making.
The best-known example of a parasite changing its host’s behavior is the “zombie ant” fungus, Ophiocordyceps, which helped inspire “The Last of Us.”

The life cycle of the zombie ant fungus begins when fungal spores land on an ant. The spores stick to the ant’s outer surface and eventually break through it, allowing the fungus to enter the body. Once inside, the fungus grows and spreads while the ant is still alive. The infection can develop over several weeks before the most dramatic changes in the ant’s behavior begin.

Eventually, the infected ant leaves the colony and begins wandering and climbing vegetation. This behavior moves the ant away from its normal habitat and into a location that favors fungal reproduction and dispersal. Near the end of the infection, the ant bites tightly onto a leaf, twig or other plant surface and remains attached in what researchers call a death grip. After the ant dies, the fungus consumes the remaining tissues and produces a stalk from the ant’s body. This structure releases spores that can fall on other ants below and begin the cycle again.

How does the fungus make the ant do this? You might imagine fungal cells invading the ant’s brain and taking control. Surprisingly, researchers examining infected ants before death found extensive fungal growth throughout the body and around muscle fibers, but not inside the brain. Fungal cells can form networks around the ant’s muscles, suggesting that the ability to manipulate behavior may involve communication between the fungus and multiple host tissues rather than direct control of the brain.

The death grip provides an especially striking example of how the fungus can manipulate its host’s muscles. The jaw muscles of infected ants are heavily colonized by the fungus, showing signs of extreme contraction. There are also signs that the fungus may be releasing molecules near these tissues. Yet motor neurons and connections between nerves and muscles can remain intact. Together, these findings suggest that the fungus may alter the machinery controlling muscle contraction rather than simply destroying it.

Scientists still do not know exactly what causes ants to undergo the entire sequence of wandering, climbing and biting. While researchers have identified fungal genes associated with proteins, toxins and other compounds that could affect chemical signaling in the host, many of these possible mechanisms have not yet been proved.

That uncertainty is part of what makes the system so fascinating. The fungus does not appear to flip a single “zombie switch.” Instead, it may change several biological systems at once until the ant behaves in a way that benefits the fungus.
Ophiocordyceps is not the only organism capable of changing a host’s behavior.

The emerald jewel wasp, Ampulex compressa, uses a very different strategy: It injects venom into a cockroach’s nervous system. The cockroach is not paralyzed, but it becomes much less likely to start moving on its own or to escape. The wasp can then lead it to a burrow and lay an egg on it.

Researchers have shown that the venom reduces activity in parts of the nervous system involved in starting movement. In other words, the cockroach can still walk, but its drive to do so has been changed.

Hairworms take behavioral manipulation one step further by leading their hosts toward their own demise. Some species infect praying mantises or crickets and grow inside them while the insect is still alive. When the worm is ready to reproduce, the infected host becomes unusually attracted to light, which may draw it toward the shiny surface of water. The host enters the water, where the worm escapes from its body and begins the next stage of its life cycle. For the host that cannot swim, that behavior can be fatal.

Researchers are still working out exactly how the parasite causes this change, but studies have found changes in proteins in the host’s brain as the parasite manipulates it. In effect, the parasite appears to hijack the host’s sensory and behavioral machinery to guide it somewhere it would not normally go.
Behavioral manipulation also occurs in mammals. Toxoplasma gondii can infect many warm-blooded animals, but it reproduces in cats.

While rodents normally avoid cat odors, those infected with the parasite can lose some of that natural aversion and even become attracted to cat odors. This change could increase the chance that an infected rodent is eaten by a cat, allowing the parasite to complete its life cycle.

These examples show why “mind control” is an imperfect description of how parasites manipulate their hosts. Parasites do not need to control every action that their host makes. They may only need to change one key behavior: whether to climb, whether to walk away, whether to enter water or whether to avoid a predator.

There is no single “zombie switch.” Behavior emerges from communication between the nervous system, muscles and other tissues throughout the body. Different parasites have evolved different ways to interfere with those systems.

So biology cannot create the dancing dead of “Thriller” or the infected humans of “The Last of Us.” But if a zombie is a living organism whose normal behavior has been redirected by another organism, nature has already created plenty of them.
Studying these real-life zombies may help scientists understand not only how parasites manipulate their hosts, but also how normal behavior is generated and controlled in the first place.

title: Democrats are the unwitting beneficiaries of Trump’s immigration policies
paragraphs: In a 2025 investigation, The New York Times reported that officials in President Joe Biden’s administration, in the wake of Biden’s 2020 election win, had viewed rising immigration as “a distraction” best ignored so that the administration could concentrate political resources on more important economic matters.

Scott Shuchart, a Biden appointee who joined the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency in 2022, told the newspaper that the White House was “wishing the problem would go away so that they could focus on the things they cared about.”

But two years after Donald Trump leveraged voter dissatisfaction with the Biden administration’s management of the U.S. southern border to win the 2024 election and enforce his immigration crackdown, the issue has suddenly become a secondary matter.

Amid the rising U.S. cost of living, a destabilizing war in Iran and a disrupted system of global commerce, the now-quiet border has relieved Democrats of their thorniest issue just in time for midterm elections.
For the past three decades, the Democratic Party and its candidates have struggled to develop and pass new immigration policies and communicate related political messages.

Bipartisan attempts at comprehensive immigration reform died on Capitol Hill in 2006, 2007 and 2013. Since then, a majority of Americans has trusted Republicans more with governing the issue. That has given the GOP an advantage when the salience of immigration policy has risen due to border crises and related high-profile events, even if that edge has recently narrowed.

In a February 2024 poll, 28% of U.S. respondents told Gallup that immigration was the country’s most important problem – matching the largest share since tracking began in 1981. By May 2026, that figure was 8%, a staggering drop in such a short period.

In a different poll by The Economist/YouGov, the share of U.S. registered voters who identified immigration as the country’s most important issue fell from 14% in October 2024 to 5% in September 2026.

Erik Iverson, a Republican Senate campaign pollster, recently told Axios that declining border crossings have reduced the urgency of immigration, depriving Republicans of an issue that previously energized voters and offered conservatives an advantage.
“You become a victim of your own success,” he said.
But this success is dubious. President Trump’s approval ratings on immigration are underwater.

In the RealClear Polling average from September to October 2026, his net approval was at negative 10.8%. In a recent Fox News poll, most Americans believe the Trump administration has “gone too far” in enforcing immigration laws, including 60% of independents.

Despite Republicans’ insistence that the mass removal of undocumented immigrants and a halt to new migrants would raise wages and make housing more accessible, Americans are experiencing high inflation rates, slow gross domestic product growth and sour consumer sentiment.

Ominously for the White House, Trump’s negative 10.8% net approval score on immigration is actually among his best. On inflation, the economy and foreign policy, his net approval rating is at negative 42.8%, negative 31.7% and negative 27.8%, respectively.
These dynamics bode well for Democrats’ midterm election prospects.

Republicans are now less concerned about immigration – what has been their greatest source of political energy and the left’s greatest political liability – as both parties’ voters are focused on other matters.

Despite the White House’s aggressive and frequently violent pursuit of undocumented immigrants, its proposal to end birthright citizenship, and its near closure of U.S. borders, even Democrats are no more likely to identify immigration as the country’s top issue today than they were previously.
According to The Economist/YouGov polling cited earlier, 1% of Democrats named immigration as their top issue in September 2026. In October 2024, 3% said the same.

Remarkably, without Democrats’ endorsement of a single new immigration policy idea, independents now express greater trust in Democrats than Republicans on immigration, 41% to 27%, according to a September 2026 Marist survey.
Democrats’ sudden edge arises after a decade of trialing different approaches to counter the nativism and popular discomfort that Trump has harnessed.

Before Trump’s 2016 election victory and immediately thereafter, Democratic leaders sought to ameliorate the image of foreigners in the U.S., by highlighting that immigrants start more businesses, file more patents and commit fewer crimes than native-born U.S. citizens on average.

During this period, Democrats commonly cited immigrants’ acute vulnerability and their willingness and ability to fill critical low-skilled and high-skilled labor gaps. But the praise and pity produced resentment among many Americans who did not want an admissions system that elevated foreigners to a higher pedestal.
Toward the end of the first Trump administration, Democrats began citing the immense macroeconomic and fiscal benefits driven by immigrants’ long-term settlement in the U.S.

Economists attribute to immigrants the bulk of U.S. population growth from 1990 to 2015. And economists have shown that continued immigration mitigates inflation and extends the solvency of Social Security and Medicare funds. Immigration also provides workers for industries like construction, agriculture, food production and healthcare.

title: Political information increasingly comes from pop culture, outside of partisan silos but where male creators – and sometimes misogyny – dominate
paragraphs: Research on political polarization points to how people’s preferred news outlets and social media use create information silos, environments in which people primarily encounter views consistent with their own, further cementing those views.
But this research often omits an important source of political information: popular culture, from influencers and podcasts to comedy, television and movies.

Politics are intertwined with popular entertainment media. The current president is a former reality television star who was reelected in 2024 with the help of comedy podcasters like Joe Rogan. Blockbuster films such as “The Odyssey” spark controversy and turn into political footballs, while late-night talk show hosts must skirt the Trump administration’s regulatory ire with their politically oriented humor.

While we know a lot about the news-consumption habits of Republicans and Democrats, there is less data about the other places that people encounter political ideas. This is particularly true for younger people, who are increasingly likely to get political content from social media influencers and popular culture sources.

Political consultant Sarah Longwell of The Bulwark recently told The New York Times’ Ezra Klein that many people in her focus groups get political information from an “algorithm-driven information environment” populated by influencers, comedians and sports personalities. She noted that the “overlap between politics and culture” creates a “vibe” that shapes many people’s political decision-making.

As co-founders and research affiliates of Colorado State University’s Center for Democracy, Art, and Popular Culture, we conducted a survey that documents the pop culture preferences of Americans ages 18-49.

We wanted to know whether the siloing that has been observed in Americans’ news environments is replicated when younger Americans are consuming entertainment media that often contains political content.
It isn’t.

That matters, because popular influencers and entertainers who cross partisan boundaries have an increased ability to shape the political “vibe” discussed by Longwell. And an important finding from our survey is that many of the favorite creators and outlets ranked in the survey feature men and promote masculinity.
Pop culture is the diverse collection of cultural productions consumed by members of a society: films, television series, video games, art, music, comedy and the like.
We asked 741 Americans to name their top influencers, podcasts, comedians, musicians, video games, films and television series. We examined results by age and political party.

Respondents first identified which pop culture outlets they engaged with and then shared their favorites in each content category. The answers were diffuse, but trends are evident in the top three listed by people across political affiliations.
Both the Democratic and Republican parties have turned to influencers to reach voters – particularly young voters – who “don’t consume traditional political news.”

In our survey’s lists of favorite influencers, three creators who rose to fame staging viral stunts, interviewing celebrities and playing video games on YouTube and the live streaming platform Twitch dominated the list: MrBeast was No. 1 for Democrats, Republicans and independents. Republicans and independents ranked Kai Cenat in their top three, while IShowSpeed was No. 2 for Democrats and Republicans.

A similar pattern of the same names populating each list is evident in people’s favorite podcasts. “The Joe Rogan Experience” and “Call Her Daddy” were in all groups’ top three, while Republicans and independents also ranked the “Tucker Carlson Show” and “This Past Weekend with Theo Von.”

Joe Rogan and Theo Von are comedians turned podcasters, whereas Tucker Carlson rose to fame as a right-wing pundit. “Call Her Daddy” is an outlier on our list insofar as it is hosted by a woman, Alex Cooper, and is known for frank discussions of sex and relationships.

The website Campaigns & Elections reported that in 2024 half of all registered voters surveyed who listened to at least one podcast per month said that podcasts had some influence on their vote. The site reported that in the 2024 presidential election, those podcast listeners favored conservatives.

Our survey helps to explain why. Rogan, popular with all three groups, has long voiced libertarian ideas and platformed right-wing politicians. Von occupies a similar space, and Carlson is conservative. Both are favorites not just of Republicans but also independents.
Political scientists and media scholars have demonstrated how comedy can influence politics. Our survey found considerable overlap among political partisans’ favorite comedians.

Dave Chappelle, creator of the boundary-breaking Comedy Central series “Chappelle’s Show,” topped the list for Democrats and Republicans and was the second favorite of independents. Bill Burr, known for comedy that is both cocky and aggrieved, was in the top three for Republicans and Democrats, while Shane Gillis, whose comedy The New York Times says “fits into the evolving meaning of conservatism,” was second and third for independents and Republicans.

Video games are another shared pop culture venue where Americans of different political affiliations are encountering one another as they play, via discussions with other players on Twitch and by participating in the comments sections of gameplay livestreams.

Researchers have demonstrated that young people, in particular, are exposed to diverse political views when engaging with one another in “online participatory activities that are non-political in nature.”

For example, one study examined how a viral trend of “building Trump’s wall” while playing Fortnite spurred political discussions both inside the game and in comments on gameplay videos and social media posts.

U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez demonstrated the political power of the medium in 2020 when she livestreamed herself playing the game Among Us, an online, multiplayer deduction game similar to the popular party games Mafia and Werewolf. Ocasio-Cortez playing the game with U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar and prominent gamers was billed as a get-out-the-vote effort and earned 4.5 million views.

title: What is Sharia law, and why is it so controversial in the United States?
paragraphs: At a campaign rally, in Port Huron, Michigan, on Oct. 25, 2026, President Donald Trump accused U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of being a “jihadist” who wants to impose Sharia law – Islamic law – in the United States. His comments reflect a broader pattern among Republican politicians of portraying Sharia as a threat to the American legal system.

In March 2026, Texas legislators launched the Sharia Free Texas Caucus, a group dedicated to preventing what its members describe as the spread of Islamic law in Texas. Its founder, state Rep. Brent Money, has characterized Sharia as “an entire civilizational legal structure” that threatens American law and institutions. That same month, nearly 95% of Texas Republican primary voters backed a nonbinding proposition declaring that “Texas should prohibit Sharia Law.” The movement extends beyond Texas. In Congress, the Sharia Free America Caucus, established in December 2025, grew to 68 Republican lawmakers from 25 states in just six months.
These efforts reflect a long-standing claim, frequently invoked by anti-Sharia activists, that Muslims are seeking to establish a parallel legal system that will eventually replace American law.
But this rhetoric raises a more basic question: What exactly is Sharia, and what does it actually mean for Muslims to follow it while living in the United States?

I am a law professor who studies religious liberty. My 2019 book, “When Islam Is Not a Religion,” examined how ordinary Muslim religious practices come to be treated as political threats, and I recently documented that pattern in Texas. The Sharia controversy shows how this happens.

In Arabic, “sharia” means a path or way, literally “the path to a watering place.” For Muslims, it refers to the divinely ordained way of living a moral and religious life, guided by the Quran and the teachings of the Prophet Muhammad.

Sharia guides Muslims how to pray, when to fast, what to eat and how much to give to charity. It also addresses marriage and divorce. These rules span what Americans would sort into law, ethics, manners and worship, as law professor and an authority on Islamic law Asifa Quraishi-Landes has explained.

This distinction matters because Americans often think of law as something established and enforced by the state. Sharia is broader than that. A Muslim who avoids pork or prays five times a day may see each practice as part of following Sharia, but neither requires a separate legal court or government enforcement.

Rules governing marriage, divorce and inheritance, by contrast, may have legal consequences, though how they are interpreted and applied varies across Islamic traditions. Indeed, as Quraishi-Landes notes, Sharia itself obliges Muslims to follow the law of the land wherever they live.

Muslims do not all agree on how Sharia should be interpreted. They distinguish between Sharia, which they regard as the divine ideal, and “fiqh,” the human effort to understand and apply it. In other words, Muslims believe Sharia comes from God, but people must figure out what it requires in practice. Because people can disagree, interpretations can differ and change over time.
Sunni Islam’s four major schools and Shiite Islam’s legal traditions sometimes reach different conclusions about matters such as marriage, divorce and financial transactions.

For example, scholars differ on whether Muslims can take out conventional mortgages to buy homes, given Islamic prohibitions on interest, and on the conditions under which a marriage can be dissolved. They continue to debate newer questions, too, such as whether organ donation is permissible or how modern banking can comply with Islamic principles.

No single institution speaks for all Muslims. Yet political debates often treat Sharia as a fixed rule book, when much of the Islamic legal tradition consists of ongoing disagreements about what its rules mean and how they should apply.

Muslims are subject to the same laws as everyone else in the United States. Their religious commitments may guide personal decisions about marriage, divorce, finances and everyday conduct, but Sharia has no independent legal authority. Muslims can follow religious rules voluntarily, but those rules cannot override American law.

This is not unique to Islam. Religious communities across the country have long used their own procedures to resolve disputes. For example, many Orthodox Jewish couples sign prenuptial agreements committing them to appear before a Jewish religious court, known as a beth din, if their marriage breaks down. The court can then help facilitate a religious divorce, including addressing situations in which a husband refuses to grant his wife a religious divorce. Christian organizations likewise offer biblical mediation and arbitration to resolve conflicts according to religious principles.

Muslims can similarly turn to religious scholars or mediators for guidance on family or financial disputes. These arrangements are generally voluntary, and any legally enforceable agreement must comply with American law.

A religious ruling does not become binding simply because a religious authority issues it. Like other religious communities, Muslims may organize aspects of their personal lives around their faith, but they do so within the framework of American law.
Critics often claim Sharia is gaining a foothold in the courts. The concern usually arises when Muslims ask a court to recognize a religious contract or arbitration.

Consider an Islamic marriage contract promising the wife a marriage gift, known as “mahr,” some or all of which may be payable if the couple divorces. A court asked to enforce it does not decide what Islamic theology requires. It asks whether the agreement meets ordinary contract law. In 2020, a Maryland appeals court held that a “mahr” could be enforced only under the same secular standards that apply to any agreement between spouses. In other words, the court’s job is to determine whether the couple’s agreement is legally enforceable, just as it would with any other contract. It is not enforcing Islamic religious law.

Courts may apply what the Supreme Court calls “neutral principles of law.” That simply means applying ordinary legal rules without deciding religious questions. A judge can determine whether two people entered into a valid contract, for example, but cannot decide which interpretation of Islam is religiously correct. As law professor Haider Ala Hamoudi has observed, courts can enforce a “mahr” agreement precisely because doing so does not require them to interpret Islamic law.

Arbitration works the same way. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has called Islamic panels “Sharia tribunals masquerading as legal courts.” Yet the Beth Din of America also structures its proceedings so civil courts can enforce its rulings, as do Christian arbitrators.

Courts can enforce voluntary arbitration awards and can also vacate them for fraud or overreach. For example, suppose a Muslim couple voluntarily agree to have a religious arbitrator resolve a financial dispute. If the arbitrator orders one spouse to pay the other US$10,000, a court may enforce that decision just as it would any other arbitration award. But if one spouse was coerced into participating or the arbitrator exceeded the authority the couple had agreed to give them, a court could set the decision aside.
A religious arbitrator cannot override a statute or the Constitution.

Some concerns stem from how certain governments enforce Islamic law. In Iran, U.N. investigators have documented escalating violence against women accused of violating hijab rules. In Afghanistan, the Taliban have issued more than 100 decrees targeting women and girls.

title: 3 major issues that Republican Byron Donalds or Democrat David Jolly will need to address as Florida’s next governor
paragraphs: After nearly three decades of Republican control of Florida, the executive office of the governor has become more powerful than ever before.
So when Florida voters choose between Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly for governor on Nov. 3, the winner will be poised to shape the state’s direction for years to come.

I’m a political scientist who has lived in Florida for almost two decades and seen the powers of the governor’s office grow. I’ve been watching how the two candidates say they will use their authority to shape policy around healthcare, education and home rule – and what help they might need from the Legislature.

One of the first choices awaiting the new governor will be whom to appoint as Florida surgeon general, a position created in 2007. The surgeon general oversees the Florida Department of Health and county health departments across the state.

The position comes with the power to declare public health emergencies, forcibly quarantine people and set vaccine mandates for illnesses such as chickenpox that fall outside the state Legislature’s framework of seven childhood vaccine mandates.

As part of his conservative remake of Florida policies, Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed the current surgeon general, Dr. Joseph Ladapo, to the position in 2021. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Ladapo emerged as a leading medical freedom advocate and vaccine skeptic.

Ladapo opposes all vaccine mandates. At the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, he recommended against COVID-19 vaccinations for healthy children and ended quarantine mandates for Florida public schoolchildren exposed to COVID-19. He also said that he wanted mRNA vaccines “not to be available to anyone” in the state.

Ladapo also proposed new Florida health rules in October 2026 to drop mandates for four vaccines required for school attendance, including chickenpox and hepatitis B. Currently, the state allows exemptions only for approved religious or medical reasons.
The Florida Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics opposes the rule change on public health grounds.

Donalds has long opposed vaccine mandates and says that he did not personally receive a COVID-19 vaccine. He supports Ladapo’s proposed rule change to reduce school vaccination mandates and says he is open to reappointing Ladapo as surgeon general.

Jolly, on the other hand, supports Florida’s current school vaccine mandates and exemptions. He says he would fire Ladapo on Day 1 in favor of someone who “embraces science and evidence-based public health.”

No matter which candidate is elected governor, the Florida Legislature has tied his hands on how far he can push vaccine policy. The Legislature has mandated measles and polio vaccines for all K-12 public school students, so getting rid of that requirement would require a change in the law. It also stripped the surgeon general of the power to enforce vaccine mandates during public health emergencies in November 2021, during the pandemic.

One of the biggest developments in Florida K-12 education in recent years has been the creation of a system of universal vouchers by DeSantis and the Legislature in 2023. This program allows parents of any income level to use US$8,000 in state money on average, based on county of residence, for their children’s private or homeschooling education.

The universal voucher program has created intense pressure on the state budget. It cost an estimated $4.5 billion in fiscal year 2026. State auditors have identified accountability problems in tracking funds through the system. Public schools have faced declining enrollment, with fewer resources to serve the neediest students they cannot turn away.

Donalds strongly supports the universal voucher program, recounting how his family saved money for him to attend a private high school. Donalds has touted universal vouchers in Christian nationalist circles and expressed an interest in making Florida “the model state for school choice” by allowing parents to choose among private educational providers competing in the marketplace.
His wife, Erika Donalds, is a former Collier County school board member who operates a network of for-profit charter schools and advocates nationally for school choice.

The only change Donalds has proposed is a universal scorecard for the voucher program so that parents can compare educational data on student performance across different types of schools. Currently, only public schools must provide this data.

Jolly also supports the universal voucher program but wants significant changes. Jolly personally sends his own two children to private, faith-based schools with the support of vouchers. He says private schools that accept vouchers should meet the same standards and requirements as public schools, including the mandate to serve students with disabilities. He also wants to limit private school tuition to the value of the voucher and reinstate benefit eligibility based on financial need.
Campaign promises aside, neither candidate can do much to affect the universal voucher program, because it was created by the Legislature.

Democrat Jolly knows he would need the Legislature’s cooperation to advance reforms and claims that he has identified Republican allies to do so. Donalds would likely face a friendly Republican majority for his more modest proposed reforms.

The next Florida governor will also be able to influence state education policy by appointing the seven members of the Board of Education and then recommending a candidate for commissioner of education for that board to elect. The commissioner and state board oversee the Florida Department of Education and programs from kindergarten through postsecondary education.
The position of commissioner used to be elected, but in 2002 voters approved a constitutional amendment creating the current system, which gives more power to the governor.

The next governor’s appointees to the Board of Education could try to shape the effects of universal vouchers more indirectly. The board could approve an annual legislative budget request with new recommended funding levels for public education to make up for shortfalls due to revenue loss from vouchers.
They could also implement new eligibility rules for private school vouchers, as the DeSantis administration has done.

title: Israel has voted, but what comes next? Dissecting a messy ballot and coalition-building process
paragraphs: The Israeli election of Oct. 27, 2026, was among the most highly anticipated votes in the country’s history. It was consequential, if not yet conclusive.

With nearly all the votes counted, it is still unclear who will lead the country following the first national ballot since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack, and the devastating wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran that Israel has launched since.

The Conversation turned to Dov Waxman, an expert on Israeli politics at the University of California, Los Angeles, to walk us through the main takeaways and the process and difficulties facing anyone trying to form a coalition government following a divided vote.

The first thing to note is simply the massive turnout – with a 77.7% turnout of those eligible voting, the highest turnout in more than two decades. That in itself is significant. It underscores how much importance Israelis attached to this vote.
Before the election, many observers were saying that it was one of the most consequential – if not the most consequential – votes, and clearly many Israelis felt the same way.
What drove this high turnout was different types of fears. Israelis of all persuasions were worried about how the outcome would affect what kind of country Israel becomes.

The second big takeaway is that the ruling coalition, formed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after the 2022 election, was resoundingly rejected by the majority of Israeli voters – well over 50% cast their vote for parties opposed to the current government.

The five parties that make up Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious coalition went into the election with 68 seats in the 120-seat parliament. That same bloc will now have 53 – and that is a significant loss, no matter how Netanyahu tries to spin this as a victory.
It means that those five parties will not be able to form the next government, and as such, the vote stands as a repudiation of the Netanyahu government.

Netanyahu’s Likud party will still be the largest in parliament. But its share of the national vote declined, and it looks like it will have six fewer seats in the next parliament, another blow to Netanyahu.

Netanyahu’s far-right coalition partners fared worse than expected, too. In part, this was due to “wasted votes” going to a new far-right party that failed to make it above the 3.25% of the national vote needed to be represented in parliament. Also, Likud drew some voters away from these far-right parties who had voted for them in the last election.
The performance of the Arab majority parties – the more secular and left-wing Joint List and the more religious and conservative United Arab List – is very important.
Combined, they currently look to have increased their representation by nine seats, bringing their total to 19, a historic high for them.

The reason for that is the massive turnout of Arab voters – much higher than the last election. But also, a less noticed trend is the increase in Jewish votes that those parties received. It is important to note that these are Arab-majority parties, not simply Arab parties.

Aside from Netanyahu, it was also a disappointing result for the main opposition party, Yashar; its leader, Gadi Eisenkot; and the anti-Netanyahu Change Bloc it was part of. The preelection polls suggested that the Zionist opposition bloc would do slightly better than the ruling coalition bloc.
But Yashar ended up with over 200,000 fewer votes than Likud, winning a projected 21 seats compared to Likud’s 26, and the “Change Bloc” is heading to 48 seats, far short of a parliamentary majority.

Ultimately, what is clear is that the Israeli public remains deeply divided. And the fact that there is still a good chance that Netanyahu will emerge as prime minister is remarkable given that many observers had already written his political obituary after the Oct. 7 attack.
Certainly many saw this as a referendum on Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.

For his supporters, Netanyahu is the only person to be trusted with Israel’s security, especially given the threat from Iran. They credit him for weakening – albeit not defeating – the two non-state actors that most threaten Israeli security, Hezbollah and Hamas, and they praise him for ensuring President Donald Trump’s support for Israel.

But for those who voted against Netanyahu, the fact that he has refused to take any personal responsibility for the Oct. 7 security failure – amid reports that he had advance warning of a major planned Hamas attack – factored into his poor election showing, as did his government’s refusal to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the Oct. 7 security failings.

Many also blame Netanyahu for not prioritizing the release of the Israeli hostages held in Gaza and prolonging the war there. He is also held responsible by many for the precipitous decline in Israel’s international standing and for jeopardizing Israel’s crucial alliance with the United States.

But it was domestic issues, rather than external ones, that motivated many of those who voted for anti-Netanyahu parties. Many fear that democracy in Israel is under attack, and they particularly oppose the effort by Netanyahu’s government to weaken the power and independence of the Israeli judiciary, which sparked massive street protests in 2023. They also strongly resent that Netanyahu’s government has allowed ultra-Orthodox men to avoid military service, despite the Israeli military’s growing manpower shortage. And on a personal level, Netanyahu is widely perceived as self-serving and dishonest – he is still on trial for corruption.

Arab voters have other, more specific concerns that drove them to vote in record numbers, in addition to the Netanyahu government’s policies in Gaza and the West Bank, which they strongly oppose. Chief among them is the soaring rates of violent crime in their communities, which the government – particularly the far-right Itamar Ben-Gvir, who oversees the police – has done nothing to address, say his critics. More broadly, many Palestinian-Arab citizens of Israel fear that if the far-right parties remained in power, their civil rights would be under threat.

The key thing to underline is what happens on election day in Israel is just the first stage in the process of forming a new government. Since no party ever receives a majority of seats in the parliament, what really matters is what happens after the election when the coalition building begins. This can take weeks, if not longer.

title: King Charles’ visit to the Caribbean evokes specter of British slavery – and local demands for justice
paragraphs: King Charles III touched down in the Bahamas on Oct. 27, 2026, with far more baggage than usual. The nine-day trip in the Caribbean also features stops for the U.K. monarch in Guyana and in Antigua and Barbuda for the annual Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting.

The king’s royal tour comes amid mounting Caribbean demands for reparations and renewed scrutiny of the British monarchy’s historical role in slavery. These developments have intensified debate in Caribbean Commonwealth realms over whether to retain the British monarch as head of state.

Anticipating local calls for a royal apology, Buckingham Palace telegraphed ahead of time that Charles would not formally apologize for slavery on behalf of the British government during the visit. King Charles started his tour noting the “great suffering of the past,” but Buckingham Palace has said previously that the legacies of colonialism and slavery are matters “primarily for governments to address.”
It is a familiar formula for the Crown: acknowledge the horrors of the past, express sorrow and leave responsibility unanswered.

Both as heir apparent and now as king, Charles has spoken about the atrocity of slavery during visits to Ghana, Barbados, Rwanda and Bermuda. Such acknowledgment matters, particularly when historical injustices have been repeatedly minimized or excluded from official narratives.

But as a historian focused on Britain’s Atlantic slave empire, I believe that expressions of regret cannot substitute for meaningful engagement with the demands of those whose ancestors were enslaved. The king’s Caribbean visit is an occasion to recognize the full story of Britain’s trafficking and enslavement of millions of Africans across the Atlantic – and the Crown’s direct culpability.
While Buckingham Palace today says it is up to the government to litigate questions of historical justice, the monarchy was no passive participant in the Atlantic slave system.
Alongside the work of other historians, my recent book, “The Crown’s Silence,” documents the monarchy’s direct involvement in the expansion and administration of Britain’s Atlantic slave empire.

Beginning in 1563 with the reign of Elizabeth I, the monarchy invested in transatlantic slaving voyages, granted monopoly charters to slave-trading companies, provided Royal Navy vessels for convoy protection of slaving vessels, and profited from the expansion of slavery in the Atlantic world.

Successive monarchs relied heavily on customs revenue derived from enslaved labor and endorsed colonial laws categorizing enslaved people as property – to be bought, sold, mortgaged, seized for debt and inherited. Enslaved men and women were also purchased in the Crown’s name to labor at Royal Navy dockyards and serve in the West India Regiments.
The paper trail of royal complicity in slavery thus stretches across three centuries.

The financial settlement that accompanied Britain’s abolition of slavery in 1834 makes the injustice particularly stark. The British state compensated enslavers $26.6 million (approximately $4.5 billion today) for the loss of their so-called human property.

In contrast, the formerly enslaved received no restitution for generations of stolen labor and lives, extreme brutality and family separation. The consequences extended well beyond emancipation, shaping patterns of land ownership, wealth, racial inequality and economic dependency that continue to affect Caribbean societies and members of the African diaspora today.
This history is central to understanding why reparatory justice remains a pressing demand.

Reparations transcend apologies and requests for monetary compensation. In June, the African Union and CARICOM, the intergovernmental organization covering more than a dozen Caribbean nations, agreed to a 19-point reparations plan that calls for, among other things, formal apologies, debt relief, financial reform, cultural restitution and the establishment of an international reparatory justice fund.

The Caribbean has advanced a comprehensive case for reparations targeting Britain and other European colonial powers for years. In 2014, CARICOM’s reparations initiative gained momentum – but efforts to pursue claims against the British government met legal resistance, including a successful challenge that the claim lacked jurisdiction. The demand has nonetheless persisted, exposing for countries in question the inadequacy of indefinitely postponing reparations through diplomatic language.

The Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, Nov. 1-4, 2026, offers another test of the Commonwealth, which comprises 56 member states, the majority of which were once part of the British Empire, and its commitment to equality. The organization describes itself as a voluntary association of independent states united by shared goals and values. Yet that ideal sits uncomfortably alongside the afterlives of slavery and empire.

Caribbean countries are attempting to participate as equal partners, while Britain, the former imperial center, resists meaningful engagement with the historical foundations of its wealth and power. As Shirley Botchwey, the Commonwealth’s secretary-general, recently remarked, the “time has come” for the king to apologize for slavery and discuss reparations.

The Crown’s position on this issue extends beyond what Charles does or does not say in a speech. That, to critics, is evident in the boundaries imposed on the discussion: The king may condemn slavery, but he leaves the monarchy’s institutional responsibility unaddressed; he may express sorrow for colonial atrocities, but reparations are left to governments that refuse to consider them.

As new historical research has further documented Britain’s involvement in slavery, the United Nations in March 2026 declared slavery “the gravest crime against humanity.” In September, Jamaica submitted a petition asking Charles, as Britain’s head of state, to refer questions about the legality of slavery, its compatibility with international law and Britain’s potential obligation to provide a remedy to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council – Britain’s final court of appeal for overseas territories and Crown dependencies.

The petition represents the first time a Commonwealth realm has sought a legal determination on the legality of Britain’s trafficking and enslavement of Africans. On Sept. 22, the king referred the petition to the Privy Council, which has set a preliminary hearing for March 2027.

Charles could have declined the referral, and the move provides a route for legal consideration of questions long resisted by Britain. But it also illustrates the monarchy’s contradictory position. The king’s constitutional role can facilitate a pathway for Jamaica’s reparations petition, even as the Palace invoked constitutional limitations to temper expectations during the Caribbean royal tour.
Consequently, while the referral marks a significant procedural step, it’s still, on its own, insufficient, according to reparations activists.

Unless the king takes more substantive action, his position as head of state in multiple Caribbean countries is at risk. Since Charles’ accession in 2022, several Commonwealth realms have renewed discussions about becoming republics. Following Barbados’ removal of the British monarch as head of state in 2021, Jamaica, the Bahamas, Antigua and Barbuda and others have reconsidered their own constitutional arrangements.

title: School librarians are vanishing from Michigan schools just when they are needed most
paragraphs: Fewer than 10% of Michigan public schools report having a school library staffed with a trained school librarian.

Although Michigan strongly recommends that schools employ certified librarians, the state does not require them. In the 2023–24 school year, the state ranked 46th in the student-to-librarian ratio, with one school librarian for every 2,760 students.

The lack of school librarians impacts students across Michigan, but particularly in low-income communities like Detroit and Flint and more isolated ones like Alcona County in the northern Lower Peninsula and Ontonagon in the Upper Peninsula, exacerbating disparities in resources for young people.

We are scholars in library and information sciences from Wayne State University, studying information access and ethics and equity in education and school libraries. Currently, we are conducting a statewide campaign to contact every school in Michigan and learn about their libraries, staffing, book collections, technology resources and more.

Michigan’s 2025–26 School Aid budget funded our statewide survey to measure the school librarian shortage and guide efforts to address it. Our work, and the work of many others, reveals how school librarians help students become strong readers and informed citizens.

A missing librarian is harder to see than an empty bookshelf. A room full of books can look like a school library. But if students cannot borrow those books, teachers have no librarian to plan lessons with, and no one leads author visits or digital citizenship lessons, the space offers only a fraction of what a school library can provide.

School librarians bring those services to life. Also called school library media specialists, they hold a teaching certificate and complete advanced education. They connect students with books they want to read and work with teachers to build richer lessons, using library resources to extend learning beyond the textbook.

Their impact stretches far beyond standardized test scores, though studies link strong library programs with higher student achievement and improved student literacy, especially for struggling readers. They can instill a love of reading and teach technological skills, which is critical in the age of artificial intelligence.

At our Michigan School Census symposium held in 2026, Michigan school librarians and a principal described what that work looks like. Brian Peck, a teacher librarian at Detroit’s UPrep Academy, helped students research and build a library where none had existed. He reported that 334 students voluntarily visited and checked out books during the previous school year.

At West Ottawa, librarian Julia Reynolds described replacing crowded shelves with displays that let children see book covers. Circulation quadrupled, she reported. A principal on the panel explained how district support helped schools make library visits a priority from the first week of school.
Access to information is only a start. Students also need help making sense of what reaches them through searches, social media and AI.
AI can create convincing fake videos of students doing or saying things they never did, harming their reputations and undermining trust in what people see online.

Less visible forces shape students’ information worlds, too. Algorithms and online platforms often dictate which search results and suggested videos appear first. Students need to understand that the first result is not necessarily the most credible or trustworthy source. AI is becoming so prominent that even elementary school students are learning about it.
Information literacy means knowing how to find, judge and use information. School librarians turn those skills into practice.
For a history assignment, a librarian might help students compare a newspaper account with a firsthand record. Who produced each source? What might explain their different accounts?
The same habits apply to AI. Students can trace a claim to its source, check whether the source exists and compare what it says with the generated answer. A confident response still needs evidence.

Guided by certified school librarians, students can build upon these foundations and learn to effectively find, evaluate and use information, including news articles about a historic event for a social studies assignment or to analyze current social media trends. Students can also judge the accuracy, recency and relevance of information. They learn to apply information in decision-making, writing and other forms of communication.
Knowing whether information is trustworthy is an important skill. Deciding what to do with it is another.
Digital citizenship includes deciding whether to post someone’s photo, seeking their permission before doing so, and choosing not to share a fake video.
Recent research emphasizes that digital citizenship prepares students to be empowered online and act ethically, safely and legally in digital environments.
Our work also starts with the knowledge young people bring to school.

Project Restoring Urban School Libraries helped classroom teachers earn the additional endorsement needed to become school librarians. The program combined mentoring with coursework that drew on students’ cultures, including using hip-hop to explore how young people find, create and share information.
Students start by examining the media they already use. A lesson might ask them to trace a sample, credit its creator and discuss what changes when someone else’s work reaches a new audience.

Principal preparation programs can help school leaders understand what school librarians contribute beyond book checkout. But principals and school librarians often train in separate academic units: colleges of education and schools of library and information science. Without shared coursework or joint projects, principals may complete their training without learning how to work with a school librarian.

title: Earwax is both slippery and sticky – this weird combo might lead to safer insect repellents
paragraphs: Here’s a bit of a riddle for you: What has the consistency of both toothpaste and dough, can absorb twice its weight in water and still remain sticky, was used by medieval artists as a binder in paint and has been hypothesized by physicians to repel insects?
It’s earwax.

The medical term for earwax is cerumen, based on keros, the Greek word for beeswax. People have been pondering earwax since ancient times. Ancient hygiene kits including picks and spoons to remove earwax have been found in archaeological sites worldwide.

Even today, it remains a perpetual question: to remove or not to remove your earwax? The answer: Don’t do it. The general medical belief is that ears are self-cleaning, and earwax brings benefits such as lubricating the ear canal, fighting infection and acting like a sticky net to trap debris before it reaches the eardrum. By poking in there you can accidentally make matters worse, pushing wax deeper or scratching your delicate ear canal.

Cerumen impaction – or blocked earwax – affects about a fifth of the American population, leading to 12 million patient visits per year. Blockages are worsened by daily activities such as wearing earbuds or hearing aids.

Another common problem with ears is wedged debris. For children, much of this is self-inflicted, in the form of items such as Legos or erasers. But for many adults who have something stuck in their ear, the debris is insects, such as ants, beetles, flies or cockroaches.

While rare for the average person, insects in the ear occurred with such frequency over the years that physicians began to wonder whether earwax evolved as a natural barrier for insects. But how would such a barrier work?

To answer this question, my Ph.D. student David Ancalle led experiments with earwax and insects. We teamed up with Yuhang Hu and her student Donjing He, experts in the behavior of soft solids such as hydrogels. As mechanical engineers, we wanted to focus on the physics rather than the chemistry of earwax.
Our research, published in the journal Soft Matter, shows that earwax can, in fact, stop insects without the use of dangerous chemicals.
To do experiments, we needed voluminous amounts of earwax.

Initially we obtained earwax from deceased mammals such as pigs, sheep and rabbits. Eventually we turned to our friends and family. A person has only a grain of rice’s worth of earwax in each ear. Due to a mutation in a single gene, East Asians have dry, flaky earwax, while people of African or European descent have wet, squishy earwax.

To simulate an ant climbing into an ear canal, we used a glass beaker with its rim coated in earwax. Ants, like many insects, are climbing specialists, capable of traveling across many kinds of surfaces. To climb rough surfaces, ants have spikes on their feet, like mountain climbers do, that helps them grasp onto ridges and cracks. For smooth surfaces, ants unfurl wet suction cups, which can support 60 times their body weight on smooth glass.
Watching ants trying to climb earwax showed us how strange a substance it really is. Rough earwax slowed them down, but with their claws they made progress.
But as soon as ants tried to climb smooth earwax, they fell immediately.
From these experiments, we concluded that earwax had anti-stick properties when in contact with the insects’ feet.

We next conducted experiments with ants crawling through an earwax-coated tunnel, more similar in size to a human ear canal. As the ants attempted to travel through the tunnel, earwax stuck to them. Once coated, they groomed furiously, unwilling to walk until they had removed as much as possible. Even after several minutes of effort, the ants still had earwax sticking to hard-to-reach places.

So, earwax is a paradoxical material: It is simultaneously slippery, thanks to the lipids it contains, but also sticky. Similar to many materials – including ketchup, paint and shampoo – it thins out when it is physically deformed, what physicists call shear-thinning.

The dual qualities of earwax have to do with its unique composition. Earwax is made up of flakes of skin cells held together with a binder. This blend forms a kind of sponge with microscopic holes. When a body overproduces earwax, it heaps up in boulders that ants can easily climb over.

When the substance is smooth, however, ants rely on their wet suction cups. The holes in the earwax absorb the drops produced by the ants, preventing them from attaching. Absorbency makes earwax fundamentally different from commonly used forms of pest control.

In your local store, you will find sticky surfaces such as fly paper or chemicals that kill the insects. Some researchers look to nature to find bio-friendly alternatives to using chemicals; for example, plants have properties that prevent insects from climbing.
From this study, we learned that the ear is also a model for insect repellency. Earwax is made of natural materials but has a structure that prevents ants from sticking to it.

The porosity of earwax also gives it unique properties. We showed it can absorb twice its weight in water yet still cling to the walls of the ear. This water-absorbing ability may help prevent water from accumulating on the delicate eardrum and fend off infections such as swimmer’s ear.
Scientists don’t yet understand the complex relationship between earwax, water and bacteria. Some studies show that earwax kills bacteria, but other studies find that earwax harbors bacteria.

Our experiments showed that earwax is most challenging to insects when similar to the thin layer of earwax maintained by a healthy human body. Wax would accumulate more in human ears if not for two self-cleaning mechanisms. The skin in the ear canal grows outward like a conveyor belt. Over 8-10 weeks, this process – called epithelial migration – pushes the oldest earwax out of the ear.

title: How religion collided with race and politics in Brazil’s presidential election
paragraphs: Since Brazil’s runoff elections, most attention has been focused on President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s surprise upset.

The first round of voting gave a narrow lead to challenger Flávio Bolsonaro – son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is now serving a 27-year sentence for efforts to overturn the 2022 election. In a Oct. 25, 2026, comeback, however, Lula won nearly 52% of votes, compared with the younger Bolsonaro’s 48%.

Yet the close results still highlight the country’s deep polarization, including religious divides, which have played an increasingly important role in its politics. According to polls before the election, Catholics were more likely to support Lula, while evangelicals staunchly backed Bolsonaro.

But Brazil’s evangelicals have diverse beliefs and identities. As a political scientist who studies Latin America, I believe the full picture of how faith shapes the country’s politics is more complicated – especially when it comes to race.

According to the latest national census, 57% of Brazilians are Catholic and 27% are evangelical. That is a stark shift from just 30 years ago, when 8 in 10 Brazilians considered themselves Catholic and 1 in 10 were evangelical.

Beyond Christianity, 1% of Brazilians practice Candomblé or Umbanda, which draw on African religions. Two percent follow Spiritism, a movement that took root in Brazil around the turn of the 20th century. Four percent belong to other religions, and 9% have no religious affiliation.
One measure of evangelicals’ growing influence is political. Almost 1 in 5 members of Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of Congress, identify as “evangelical.”

Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, Michelle, helped cement his support among many evangelicals ahead of his 2018 election victory. His slogan of “God, country, family and freedom” won endorsements from key clergy. As Flávio, his son, ran in the 2026 election, he also talked about religion, such as declaring that Brazil belongs “to the Lord Jesus Christ.”

But not all evangelicals are the same. Latin Americans often consider anything Christian but not Catholic to be “evangelical.” One wing of Protestant churches in Brazil is decidedly conservative and shares characteristics with evangelical churches in the United States. However, the category also includes denominations such as Methodists, Lutherans and Presbyterians.
Then there are Pentecostal groups like the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God and The Assembly of God, Brazil’s largest non-Catholic denomination.

Survey data from ISER, a Brazilian think tank focused on religion, shows that members of Pentecostal and evangelical churches are more likely to reject Lula’s Workers’ Party than any another faith group, while practitioners of African-rooted religions are more likely to reject Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party than any other group.
Surveys and research also show clear political trends around race, contrary to long-standing beliefs among many Brazilians that race does not matter in their society.

Forty-five percent of Brazilians identify as Pardo, or “Brown,” referring to people with multiracial ancestry. Forty-three percent identify as white, and 10% as Black. Around 0.6% are Indigenous, and 0.4% are East Asian.
Black Brazilians are more likely to support Lula, while those identifying as white tend to support Bolsonaro, and people identifying as Brown are evenly divided.

Examining the intersection of religion and race is also important to understanding Brazil’s diversity. About half of Black Brazilians are Catholic, and nearly 1 in 3 are evangelical; in fact, within Pentecostal and evangelical churches, a majority are of African descent.

Independent Black Christian denominations did not emerge in Brazil the way they did in the U.S.; those churches’ creation was, in part, a result of segregation. However, Black groups within religious organizations have long been involved in activism to address racism and Black communities’ concerns. Despite these efforts, leadership in both Catholic and evangelical circles has remained largely white.

During the late 2010s, a new generation of activists took the helm, concerned about intolerance toward Afro-Brazilian religions and growing Christian nationalism, and some started to more vocally criticize the Bolsonaro administration. During the 2022 election, 14 evangelical organizations created a “Brazilian Black Protestant Manifesto” calling for the government to not favor any one religion, policies to address police violence against Black youth, women’s rights and other issues.

In 2025, political scientist Gladys Mitchell-Walthour and I attended the Enegrecer Conference in São Paulo, which brought together 400 Afro-Brazilian evangelical laity and clergy calling for racial justice and progress in reducing socioeconomic inequality. A key point was rapprochement with Candomblé and Umbanda, whose places of worship are often vandalized and damaged. Ivanir dos Santos, a priest or “babalawo” in the Candomblé tradition, blessed the closing service.

Throughout the current Brazilian election cycle, religion has become a polarizing force in its own right. For example, on Instagram, one will see posts like “Real Christians don’t vote for Lula,” or “I’m Christian, and I support Lula.”

Evangelical support for Jair Bolsonaro has been a prominent feature of all recent elections. But this time, it was less unusual to see evangelicals publicly support the left – many of them Preto or Pardo.

“Christians for Democracy,” for example, a group affiliated with Lula’s party, brought together prominent Black evangelicals and Catholics on panels and held prayer rallies. The group’s Instagram page highlighted prominent leaders of Lula’s campaign who are evangelical Christians, including former Environment Minister Mariana Silva, pastor and legislator Henrique Vieira, Attorney General Jorge Mesias, legislator and former Rio de Janeiro Gov. Benedita da Silva, and André Janones. Janones, a legislator from one of Brazil’s most populous states, was the head of “Lula’s Army,” the 10 million-member WhatsApp group that was pivotal in Lula’s victory.

Lula’s victory is just one more example of how race intersects all facets of Brazilian society, including religion. I believe these durable divisions will mark Brazil’s political and religious landscape for the foreseeable future.
John Thomas III is affiliated with the African Methodist Episcopal Church.

title: Ghost stories don’t just scare us – they remind us of historical injustices
paragraphs: Along with the pumpkins and costumes, the candles and cobwebs, Halloween is all about storytelling. From tales of haunted houses to accounts of demonic possession, ghost stories are part of the holiday’s appeal.

As a professor at the University of Maine who specializes in ghost stories, I’ve thought a lot about what makes one unforgettable. My field research has taken me from the coast of Maine to the Amazon jungle, but some factors remain constant in an unforgettable tale.
One factor is what I call “creep value,” which includes the scare factor but also the elements of a story that might be simply unsettling or uncanny.

Take, for starters, the ghost of Catherine’s Hill along the Blacks Woods Road in Maine. The story warns that, against all intuition, even a lone driver at night must always stop and offer the phantom woman a ride. If not, as the story goes, she will appear when least expected in the back seat of the car to cause a fatal accident.
