But there is more to account for than creep value in an unforgettable ghost story. These stories can keep alive the memory of a dark past. In my research I have come across tales that preserve memories of injustices that might otherwise have been forgotten.
One story, about a ghost ship that can be heard but never seen, preserves the little-known history of the smuggling of enslaved people.

The legend goes that on foggy nights, during the full moon, those standing at the Cooksey Drive Overlook in Seal Harbor, just outside Acadia National Park, can hear the slaves in the hold of a sinking ship crying for help.

The story goes back to the Pride of the Seas, a ship that smuggled enslaved Africans into the United States after the trans-Atlantic slave trade had been abolished but slavery remained legal. The account specifies that the smugglers scuttled the ship to evade the law. In ghost stories that circulate by word of mouth on Mount Desert Island, the screams of those left behind can still be heard.

Pennsylvania coal miners offer another example of past grievances passed down in the form of ghost stories. At the sites of deadly accidents, people have reported the sound of a pickaxe or the groans of a dying man. An extensive archive contains multiple accounts of coal miners witnessing ghostly knocking, disembodied voices and apparitions of mangled men. One story involves an innocent coal miner, condemned to death in 1877, who left a handprint in his cell at the Carbon County Jail that no amount of sanding or paint has been able to erase.

Today, it is widely known that coal miners of the 19th and early 20th centuries experienced ruthless exploitation and hazardous working conditions. Years ago, their plight went unrecognized in official histories and government policies, but ghost stories helped keep these experiences in the collective memory.
When I collected ghost stories in South America, the same pattern held true: Some tales preserved history that would otherwise be lost.

In the Amazon jungle of northern Brazil, I traveled to a gloomy site where people, over several generations, have claimed to see the spirits of young men in the murky water. These stories keep alive injustices from the 19th century involving enslavement of Indigenous people. The location was a former sugarcane plantation notorious for cruelty, and accounts of apparitions in the water are a reminder of this history.

In Rio de Janeiro a well-known ghost story involves the apparition of a young girl in a mansion known as the Castelinho do Flamengo. All the accounts of her story agree that this young heiress, named Maria de Lourdes Fernandes, witnessed the deaths of her parents; her guardian then locked her up and drove her to suicide to get her inheritance.

Her soul is said to remain in the mansion she tried to escape. The tale is not just about an individual tragedy but one that exposes inequities involving the mistreatment of juveniles and the corrupting influence of power.
Ghost stories don’t simply recount memories – they can revive them and bring the past back into the present.
The unsolved 1898 murder of a 52-year-old woman, Sarah Ware, in Bucksport, Maine, illustrates how ghost stories can have historical significance and flood the present with the past.

In the 1980s a woman and her daughter began having nightmares about a long-haired woman in a long dress struggling to rise from the bottom of a lake. When they realized they were having the same recurring dream, they partnered with an author, and their research led them to a conclusion that the apparition was the ghost of Ware.

Official records document that when Ware’s body was recovered it was badly decomposed and her head had completely detached. Her head remained in the courthouse until the 1990s, when it was buried in Ware’s grave. According to local lore, however, Ware’s headless body is not in that grave but instead in her original grave, now located at the bottom of Silver Lake. In the oral history of the area, workers moved only the tombstones when they flooded the paupers’ graveyard – the cemetery for the poor – to make a reservoir in the 1930s.

Ware’s ghost is believed to have appeared again in 2006. When a young woman went scuba diving in Silver Lake in Bucksport, she reported seeing a woman in a long dress struggling to rise from the bottom of the lake. When she swam over to help, the figure’s hair floated back with the movement of the water to reveal she was a faceless apparition. The sighting of the faceless ghost revived the history of the unsolved murder all over again.

Ware’s case highlights the violence and injustice and their connection to gender and social class in 19th-century Maine. Missing evidence and recanted testimonies suggest that powerful men might have interfered with the investigation to hide their own complicity in the murder. As an independent woman of the time, Ware was the subject of gossip, and the treatment of her body shows how social class affects even the honoring of the dead. As a ghost story, the history of Sarah Ware is not past but rather part of the here and now.

So when you’re out and about telling ghost stories this Halloween, remember that the unforgettable ones are all about creep value in the context of a dark history that flows back in again like the tide.
Marcus Librizzi previously received funding from the Maine Humanities Council.

title: How Lula turned the tables on the right in Brazil and the US with his comeback presidential victory
paragraphs: A leader who stood up to U.S. President Donald Trump just won an election in Latin America’s biggest country, reversing a trend of new right-wing governments in the region over the past two years.

Incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, having narrowly lost to Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of voting on Oct. 5, 2026, staged a remarkable comeback on Oct. 25. He erased the deficit and won the all-important runoff election by more than 3.5 percentage points – more than 4 million votes.

It was a stunning result for the leader who proved to be the first Brazilian candidate to win a presidential election after not winning the first round, and who had been all but written off for a possible win. As a professor of Latin American politics, I believe the result offers a number of key political lessons for Brazil, Latin America – and even the United States.

The choice in the second-round election was stark. Lula offered measures to ameliorate steep income inequalities and an economy built on a transition to clean energy, environmental protection and increased access to higher education and technical training. On international matters, Lula balanced defending Brazilian sovereignty from a Trump administration keen on meddling in Latin America, and maintaining good relations with an array of nations and blocs, including the European Union and China.

Bolsonaro, meanwhile, promised sweeping cuts to government spending, more militarized policing and eager support for the Trump administration’s campaign against drug violence. His pitch also came with offers to U.S. investors of access to critical minerals in Brazil.

Such right-wing populism has been ascendant in Latin America of late, and Lula also had to overcome an anti-incumbent mood, brought on by high prices, stagnant salaries, steep interest rates and a massive corruption scandal involving Brazilian elites. That banking probe directly ensnared Bolsonaro himself, as well as powerful Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes, whom Bolsonaro’s supporters had tried to link to Lula.
Lula also had to neuter a social media landscape that has been dominated by images and narratives disparaging the president and his Workers’ Party.
Right-wing dominance of that online ecosystem helped carry Jair Bolsonaro, the 2026 hopeful’s father, to power in 2018 and got him close to reelection in 2022.
Especially after the first-round results in the 2026 vote, many analysts assumed the same pro-Bolsonaro social media presence would once again be hegemonic.
Instead, after the first round, a network of young, tech-savvy pro-Lula communicators created and shared effective, often amusing videos on WhatsApp and Instagram.

And they appealed to the center and even some of the right. All told, Lula easily made up more than 2 million votes by which he lost in the first round. He didn’t just increase turnout by millions and lower abstention rates; he also saw the state with the country’s second-largest electorate, Minas Gerais, flip to his side entirely – a swing of nearly 700,000 votes.

Emblematic of the strength of the campaign was the growth in subscribers to the WhatsApp channel Lula’s Army, which grew from 50,000 on Oct. 5 to more than 10 million by the night of the historic election.

The creator of the channel, André Janones, is a federal deputy for the Rede Party, an ally of the Workers’ Party, and a rising star in the circle around Lula. Likewise, Ana Elisa Santos Silva, a 21-year-old digital influencer and law student in the Workers’ Party, got the most votes of any federal deputy in the swing state of Minas Gerais.
A prevalent narrative of Brazilian politics has held that the country’s divisions increasingly mirror those of the United States.
Part of that idea is due to Trump’s loss in the 2020 election and the resulting attack on the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, which eerily presaged events following Jair Bolsanaro’s 2022 loss.
Like in the U.S., there has also been a rapid rise of a politically active evangelical right in Brazil.

More fundamentally, proponents of the Americanization thesis hold that U.S.-style deindustrialization and “Uberization” of the Brazilian economy have led to a decline of the unionized working class – a core support base for the left – and its replacement by an army of gig employees dreaming of owning their own businesses and throwing off the shackles of the taxing and regulating state.
Yet similarities between the two countries shouldn’t be confused for politics always moving on parallel tracks.

Survey research suggests that many Brazilians see the state as responsible for the realization of their constitutionally protected social rights, including healthcare, education and pensions. Many also regard government employment as inherently more stable and dignified than the harsh labor markets of the private sector, especially for the relatively unskilled.

For all of the apparent rise in American-style libertarian politics in Brazil, the reality is that such a viewpoint remains much smaller in the country. Flávio Bolsonaro’s bet, like his father’s before him, was that this strain of libertarian right-wing politics could nonetheless propel him to victory, much as it apparently had for Javier Milei in Argentina in 2023. But it was not enough.
Even with Lula’s win, Flávio Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party did exceptionally well at the legislative level.

When the next Brazilian Congress convenes on Feb. 1, 2027, the Liberal Party will control 28 seats in the Senate – 35% of the total; and 121 seats in the lower house – 24% of the total (as well as five governorships, which are 19% of the total).

When factoring in expected Liberal Party allies, it is clear that the right will have bigger majorities in both houses for Lula’s next administration. That will help Congress solidify control vis-a-vis the executive branch in terms of legislation and, crucially, the budget.
The election raises several questions.

title: What legal experts say about the Trump administration’s attempts to make a federal case out of state elections
paragraphs: The Trump administration’s lawsuit against Alaska, which seeks to block certification of the U.S. Senate results there if the GOP candidate does not win, is the latest in a long series of actions throughout 2026 in which the administration has attempted to wrest control of federal elections from states.

In the Alaska case, the U.S. Department of Justice, directed by President Donald Trump, claims that it aims to “protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska.” If incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan does not win reelection, the DOJ asserts, it’s likely the result of voter confusion because another candidate with a very similar name – Daniel J. Sullivan, with no party affiliation – is on the ballot, too. So in the event that Sen. Sullivan fails to win reelection, the DOJ demands that Alaska not certify the election and instead should conduct an inquest into who voters thought they were voting for.

The campaign of the Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, whose potential win in the hotly contested election could help shift the Senate to Democratic control, has called the lawsuit “wholly baseless” and “an unprecedented pre-emptive strike on democratic elections” in a court filing. Another filing states that the DOJ lawsuit “asks the Court to preemptively nullify Alaska’s U.S. Senate election and disenfranchise Alaska voters without any legal basis whatsoever. It seeks to go where law ends.”

There’s lots of other heated language in the case’s legal filings. But colorful language and legal citations are a much longer way of articulating a simple fact: The U.S. Constitution gives the president no authority over federal elections. That authority rests with the states and, to a limited degree, with Congress.
Over the past year, as the 2026 midterm elections approached, The Conversation has published a number of stories illustrating this fundamental constitutional rule. Here is a selection of them:

“States are empowered under Article 1, Section 4, of the Constitution to conduct elections and set the time, place and manner of those elections,” former federal judge John E. Jones told The Conversation in an interview on April 22, 2026. Jones was discussing Trump’s March 31 executive order to take control of mail-in voting from states and give it to the U.S. Postal Service and the Department of Homeland Security.
Jones, who is now the president of Dickinson College, explained why the framers of the Constitution set up a process in which states run elections and not the federal government:

“First of all, the federal government didn’t have the apparatus to conduct elections. And states had been running elections; they knew how to do it. There was a great deal of trust in the states’ ability to run elections. And there was the core debate of federalism, as to what powers states could retain, and they didn’t want to abdicate many of those powers,” Jones said.

There was also, Jones added, “a debate about the potential for fraud, that if there was a single entity controlling all the elections – that is, if you centralize elections under one politically motivated executive – it’s a really fraught situation which can be abused.”

“The Constitution is clear,” said Jones. “Unless amended, Article 1, Section 4 is – to use the trite phrase – what it is. The power rests with the states, absent congressional action. There is no mention of the president. None.”
Read more: Why Trump can’t just decree changes to voting by mail – a former federal judge explains how the president’s executive order is ‘a solution looking for a problem’
The Republican-controlled House also tried this year to horn in on the constitutional power of states to regulate elections and who can vote.

In February 2026, the House, urged by Trump, passed the SAVE America Act. The act would have required those registering to vote in federal elections to – in person – “provide documentary proof of U.S. citizenship.” It also required some people who were voting in federal elections to give proof of U.S. citizenship.

John J. Martin, an election law scholar at Quinnipiac University Law School, wrote that the act “presents a constitutional dilemma. By requiring individuals to show documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to vote, the SAVE America Act is implicitly saying that someone must be a U.S. citizen to vote in federal elections.”

In other words, Martin wrote, “Congress would be instituting a qualification to vote, a power that the Constitution leaves exclusively to the states. Normally, when state and federal laws conflict, the Constitution’s supremacy clause mandates that federal law prevails. Yet, in this instance, where Congress has no actual authority to implement voter qualifications, the SAVE America Act would seem to have no constitutional leg on which to stand.”
The Senate proved unwilling to pass the SAVE Act this year, so this particular constitutional battle has yet to hit the courts.
Read more: Citizenship voting requirement in SAVE America Act has no basis in the Constitution – and ignores precedent that only states decide who gets to vote

Trump frequently targets mail voting, claiming it’s rife with fraud. The March 2026 executive order by the president aimed, it said, to ensure “integrity in federal elections” by placing severe restrictions on mail voting.

Among that order’s provisions was a directive to the U.S. Postal Service to implement, election scholar Martin wrote, “uniform ballot and envelope requirements for mail and absentee ballots used in federal elections.” The order also mandated that states must “provide the Postal Service, 60 days prior to Election Day, with lists of all voters eligible to vote by mail or absentee.”

A mail ballot that didn’t comply with the Postal Service’s requirements, or was sent by somebody not on a state-provided list, would not be delivered by the Postal Service, wrote Martin, “effectively canceling that vote.”
Lawsuits were filed by a host of state officials and voting rights groups. The suits eventually made their way up to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Martin summarized their arguments: “The president does not possess unilateral authority to alter the methods of voting in federal elections. Rather, the elections clause of the Constitution vests the authority to regulate the ‘time, place, and manner’ of federal elections in the states. Congress also has the authority to regulate federal elections, if it chooses to do so.”
On Sept. 14, 2026, the Supreme Court apparently agreed, with a 7-2 vote upholding a preliminary injunction blocking the new rules.
Read more: Why the Supreme Court blocked Trump and the Postal Service from restricting mail-in voting for the midterms

title: What the failed attack on an Illinois temple reveals about anti-Hindu hate in the United States
paragraphs: Lawmakers are calling for a failed attack on the Sri Venkateswara Swami Temple in Aurora, Illinois, to be investigated as a hate crime. On Oct. 11, 2026, as hundreds of Hindu worshippers gathered for the first day of Navaratri, a celebration of the divine feminine over nine nights, a 19-year-old man traveled to the Hindu temple, armed with a rifle and body armor, according to prosecutors. A jammed gun and a tip from the suspect’s co-worker prevented a massacre. Authorities located a manifesto written by the suspect espousing white supremacist views.

U.S. Reps. Ro Khanna, a Democrat, and Rich McCormick, a Republican, warned in a letter to the FBI and DOJ that this plot “did not emerge in isolation.” They pointed to a broader rise in hostility toward Hindu Americans and Indian Americans. A 2026 Carnegie Endowment survey found that 1 in 4 Indian American adults reported being called a slur since the start of 2025.

In September 2026, for example, Bo French, a Texas Republican candidate for state office, posted a photo of a University of Texas at Austin football game that has been viewed 54 million times. Referring to the Indian American students centered in the photo, he claimed “the problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.” French’s post provoked social media responses calling for violence against Indians and desecrating Hindu temples.

French’s post said nothing about religion, yet the responses it provoked took aim at Hindu temples. As a professor of Hindu studies, I argue that this is because anti-Indian and anti-Hindu hate in the United States are deeply intertwined. Some of this hostility targets the Hindu worship of deities through sacred images, and it draws on a history of prejudice portraying Hindus as idolaters. This hate is amplified on the same online platforms that spread racial hostility.
In Hindu temples, worship centers on “murtis,” or consecrated images in which the deity is understood to be present. These temples and images have become frequent objects of online abuse.

In September 2025, Alexander Duncan, then a Republican U.S. Senate candidate in Texas, objected to a large image of the deity Hanuman in Sugar Land, Texas. He asked, “Why are we allowing a false statue of a false Hindu God to be here in Texas? We are a Christian nation!” This post was viewed over 6 million times. In August 2026, pastor Dale Partridge posted an image of the Swaminarayan Akshardham Temple in New Jersey, claiming “our 1700s Christian forefathers would have this demon temple leveled in 24 hours.”

Such rhetoric is widespread online. A September 2026 report by the Center for the Study of Organized Hate found that Hindus “have been singled out for attacks on the basis of their religion.” The report states that posts routinely refer to devotees as “demon worshippers,” deride Hindu deities and sometimes call for temples to be destroyed and replaced with “American” monuments. The report finds that these posts frame Hindu worship as “fundamentally incompatible with Christianity.”

When these posts invoke America and Christianity, they represent an outlook that sociologists Andrew Whitehead and Samuel Perry call Christian nationalism: the belief that America should be distinctively Christian. In their survey from 2017, almost a third of Americans said that the federal government should declare the United States a Christian nation.
I believe this current manifestation of Christian nationalist hostility to Hinduism is best understood in the context of the broader history of American Christian responses to Hinduism.

As religious studies scholar Michael Altman argues, the charge that Hindus worship false gods and idols took hold in American national culture nearly two centuries ago. Nineteenth-century American schoolbooks, shaped by Protestant beliefs, sorted religions into “true and false,” treating Hindu “idolatry” as proof of moral degradation.

In her study of Hinduism in America, scholar Vasudha Narayanan demonstrates that in the early 20th century, some Americans embraced Hindu ideas while keeping Hindus themselves at a distance. She explains that though a 1917 law barred most immigration from Asia, some Americans found inspiration in Hindu thought and yoga practices, presenting these not as Hindu but as “universal” spirituality.
Religion scholar Diana Eck estimates that after the 1965 Immigration and Nationality Act opened the door to immigrants from Asia, the population of Hindu Americans reached over 1 million by 2000.

Starting in the 1970s, these Hindus built dozens of temples. However, Eck shows that these new temples were often met with hostility. In 1983, for example, attackers desecrated a temple outside Pittsburgh, smashing sacred images and scrawling “Leave” on the temple altar. In the early 1990s, vandals spray-painted a future temple site in New Jersey with “Get out Hindoos.”

Religious studies scholar Sailaja Krishnamurti traces how this animosity continued into the 21st century. She points to the film “Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom,” which depicted Hindus performing human sacrifice, and to televangelists such as Pat Robertson, who denounced Hinduism as “demonic.” These depictions, she argues, are reflected in violence against Hindus. In 2019, a vandal spray-painted messages about Jesus and defaced images of Hindu deities.

The Aurora suspect’s manifesto does not single out Hindus nor does it mention “false gods.” According to U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, the manifesto describes “Indians, Jews, Black people and other minorities as ‘sub-human.’” Yet police Chief William Nord said the suspect “was looking for a large Hindu temple.” The suspect’s hatred was expressed in racial terms, but his target was a Hindu place of worship.

Education scholar Khyati Joshi calls this blending of racial and religious animosity the “racialization of religion.” In a society where whiteness and Christianity have been treated as the norm, she argues, brown skin can serve as a stand-in for a presumed “other” faith. As a consequence of this racialization, Joshi argues that “the religious nature of discrimination is overlooked.”

She gives the example of the “Dotbusters,” a gang that attacked Indian Americans in New Jersey in the 1980s. While newspapers called the attacks “racial beatings,” the gang’s name referred to the “dot” worn by Hindu women.

Krishnamoorthi, who was inside the temple with his family on the day of the attempted attack, later stated in an emotional press conference: “This shooter was radicalized by his environment. He was radicalized by social media until he told a coworker he could not wait ‘to kill Indians.’”

In tracking discrimination online, Stop AAPI Hate, a coalition tracking anti-Asian discrimination, found that South Asians were the targets of 71% of the online threats of violence against Asian groups. They note that a dominant theme of these posts was that of an “Indian invasion.”

Economists Karsten Müller and Carlo Schwarz have linked online hate to offline violence. Policy experts argue that confronting online extremism requires greater coordination across all social media companies. These scholars support a growing chorus of voices calling for accountability when hate is manifested.
Racial hatred and the demonization of Hindu gods have different sources and sometimes different voices, but on the first day of Navaratri, these forms of hate converged in a parking lot in Aurora.
In the aftermath of the failed attack, Hindu Americans are pointing to the need to speak out against both racial and religious hate.

Arun Brahmbhatt does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

title: Horror’s monsters find new meaning with queer and trans audiences – how ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ dissects identity
paragraphs: Queer horror is having a moment. The recent film “Leviticus” (2026), a harrowing allegory for conversion therapy, was a critical hit. Meanwhile, Ryan Murphy’s undeniably gay “American Horror Story” returned to TV this fall, offering a campier approach to the genre.
But queer people’s fascination with horror is by no means new. For trans and queer viewers, horror has long acted as a mirror to reflect on complex personal questions of identity and embodiment.

Another new film, Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” (2026), explores queer people’s relationship with horror. Schoenbrun’s film isn’t really a horror movie; it’s a movie about horror movies. The protagonist, a young auteur named Kris, is rebooting an old slasher franchise, “Camp Miasma.” The franchise has aged poorly, and she wants to update the film for a contemporary audience. “This part’s transphobic!” Kris mutters while watching the original film.

But Kris is also helplessly obsessed with “Camp Miasma,” and Schoenbrun’s film suggests that it’s precisely the slasher’s troubling, problematic elements that have enthralled her. As both a trans studies scholar and a longtime horror fan, I know how she feels. In fact, Kris’ complicated relationship with “Camp Miasma” may feel deeply familiar for many queer and trans viewers.

Horror has produced some of the most objectionable queer- and trans-coded characters in cinema history. These portrayals of LGBTQ+ people as monstrous and pathological can be found in films ranging from the low-budget slashers that inspired Schoenbrun – most notably “Sleepaway Camp” (1983) – to Oscar winners such as “The Silence of the Lambs” (1991).
Yet queer and trans audiences have often found themselves strangely drawn to these films and to the horror genre overall.
Why does a genre that has treated LGBTQ+ people so poorly keep them coming back?

No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps, or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.
Read more from Quarter Life:
‘Heartstopper’ is helping LGBTQ+ fans find hope and community across time and space
Childhood experiences of LGBTQ+ stigma can harm romantic relationships decades later – psychologists explain how to reconnect with yourself and your partner
Heated Rivalry shows how queer joy can disrupt hockey’s culture of masculinity
Queerness is baked into the very structure of the horror genre.

Film scholar Robin Wood summarized the horror formula as “Normality is threatened by the Monster.” As Wood points out, the social order that represents “normality” is often tied to heteronormative structures like the nuclear family and the heterosexual couple.
Horror stages gleeful attacks on this order: Think of the family under siege by malevolent spirits, or the straight camp counselors hacked to bits after having sex.
Such themes may resonate strongly for queers who find their goals and desires in tension with a society primarily built around cisgender, heterosexual life paths.
Beyond its social elements, horror also offers queer and trans people a personal encounter with an aspect of themselves that they may find confusing or even upsetting: their bodies.

Feminist scholar Carol Clover argued that horror is a “body genre,” meaning it is intended to activate a bodily response in the viewer. Often, one of the ways horror elicits this physical response is through the visceral, violent onscreen deformation of bodies.

In body horror, the human body is depicted as an unruly, often disgusting and always vulnerable accumulation of flesh, blood and guts. Such images can mirror and affirm the difficult feelings that many queer and trans folks have experienced with regard to embodiment, their distress surrounding the forms their bodies take or the desires they feel.

Horror’s depiction of monsters and monstrous bodies have allowed many queer and trans people to take ownership over their experiences of personal pain and social stigma. As trans theorist Susan Stryker put it, “I want to lay claim to the dark power of my monstrous identity without using it as a weapon against others or being wounded by it myself.”
Other queer and trans writers, however, have asked about the limits of identifying with monstrosity.

“How does building an identity on reclaiming the boogeyman affect the psyche?” wonders critic Grace Byron. Horror, after all, centers on violence, brutality, fear and even death. Identifying with these forces might feel powerful in the moment, but it doesn’t necessarily help reckon with the real violence that led LGBTQ+ people to identify with them in the first place.

When I teach horror, my students and I talk about how we might approach some of the most transphobic figures in the horror canon. Instead of identifying with these “monsters,” we try to think critically about the conditions that created them.

Take the trans-coded serial killer Buffalo Bill, from “The Silence of the Lambs.” Scholar Cael Keegan argues that “The Silence of the Lambs” raises issues of state violence against transgender people. Similarly, scholar Grace Lavery reads Buffalo Bill as a victim of medical gatekeeping, which bars lifesaving gender-related care from those who need it.

title: Human rights could improve – or worsen – based on how nations use the UN treaty against cybercrime
paragraphs: The United Nations Convention against Cybercrime is the first international treaty aimed at combating criminal acts committed online and at supporting victims of those crimes. At the initial signing ceremony on Oct. 25, 2025, U.N. Secretary General António Guterres said the convention was “a promise that fundamental human rights such as privacy, dignity and safety must be protected both offline and online.”

Civil society groups around the world, however, argue that the convention could make it easier for authoritarian governments to share information about people engaging in regular online activities. Because of vague language in the document, critics contend that governments would have the ability to criminalize legitimate online expression or other activities. Legal gray areas also heighten concerns for the protection of whistleblowers, activists, journalists, researchers and others who could be targeted by governments known to restrict civil and political rights.

Nations have until Dec. 31, 2026, to sign the convention. It will enter into force after 40 signatory states become parties to it by ratifying it at home. As of October 2026, 95 nations had signed the treaty, but only three have become parties to it.

When the convention was being drafted, the Biden administration signaled its support but acknowledged the concerns about potential misuse. The U.S. has not signed the agreement. The Trump administration has said it will continue to consider the convention. The administration has focused on promoting the United States’ own capabilities of combating cybercrime and has expressed concern about emboldening countries such as Russia and China to suppress freedom of expression and violate treaty obligations.

We are political scientists who study human rights and digital repression. Human rights organizations globally are worried that authoritarian regimes could use the convention to attack researchers, journalists, human rights advocates and people who criticize governments. A day before the convention was signed, 19 nongovernmental organizations released a joint statement urging nations to not sign or ratify the treaty. Groups such as Human Rights Watch, Freedom House, Access Now, Article 19 and others have warned that the convention’s human rights safeguards are inefficient. Weak protections risk further increases in transnational repression and global surveillance.

Every country has its own domestic law enforcement system. And while there is no international government to enforce U.N. treaties, U.N. conventions are designed to help fill this gap. They rely on cooperation among countries that have ratified an agreement by incorporating legal features to promote compliance.

When governments go through the ratification process, they adopt policies at home that reflect a treaty’s contents. But domestic interpretations of international laws often vary, which can lead to patchy protection of human rights. U.N. conventions on human rights also establish treaty bodies. They provide ways for independent experts to monitor human rights violations across all ratifying countries and to encourage more governments to join various conventions. These and other experts also participate in a process called the Universal Periodic Review, in which countries examine the human rights records of other countries every 4.5 years and provide recommendations for improvement.

Although the U.N. cybercrime convention says that human rights must be respected, it is ultimately not a human rights treaty. It falls under the U.N. Office of Drugs and Crime. Because of this, there is no treaty body to monitor violations, making abuses that fall outside of regular law enforcement activities even more difficult to track. Some examples include monitoring social media accounts of NGOs or activists, remotely installing spyware onto journalists’ cellphones and other devices, and using AI technologies against protesters and marginalized groups.

The convention does say that ratifying countries will meet periodically to improve cooperation and review implementation, but there are no stated goals about monitoring cybercrime or compliance with the convention. Another issue, which is present in all international laws, is treaty reservations, which allow governments to effectively ratify treaties while opting out of certain parts of them. The three countries that have ratified the convention as of October 2026 — Vietnam, Qatar and Azerbaijan — did not stipulate any reservations.

Monitoring how governments comply with the cybercrime convention is critical to ensuring that governments do not infringe on human rights. International NGOs, domestic civil society organizations, journalists and other human rights defenders often work to scrutinize and share information on government abuses. Some governments see such work as a threat, and they often repress them.

There has also been a steady rise in governments repressing people outside of their borders. Many governments are doing this through surveillance, monitoring social media, doxxing, creating AI deepfakes and even forcibly repatriating critics in exile and imprisoning them.

Because the cybercrime convention promotes information sharing among ratifying countries, human rights organizations are concerned that governments with bad human rights records might use shared information and cooperation to arrest human rights defenders or anybody accused of what the governments label as a serious crime. The convention does not limit the use of these powers to the set of core cybercrimes it has defined, nor does it set a standard for what it considers to be a serious crime.

Instead, it allows countries to determine for themselves what constitutes a serious crime under domestic law. In many countries, this includes activities protected under international law, such as criticism of the government, peaceful protest, same-sex relationships, investigative journalism and whistleblowing. This puts vulnerable groups at risk. For example, in countries where it is illegal to share LGBTQ+ content online, a government could activate the surveillance measures outlined in the convention to track and target community members at home and abroad under the guise of enforcing domestic law.

Secretary General Guterres said at the signing ceremony that “in cyberspace, nobody is safe until everybody is safe.” As countries consider ratifying the convention, we believe it would be wise to consider whether the agreement falls short of keeping people safe in cyberspace, and whether it might put human rights defenders, journalists, researchers and others in danger.

title: Fear-based campaign ads can grab attention, but whether they win votes is less clear
paragraphs: On a Monday night in September 1964, television viewers watched a little girl counting petals on a flower. Her voice gave way to a man counting down, and then a nuclear blast filled the screen.

The ad ran as a paid spot only once, in support of President Lyndon B. Johnson’s reelection campaign. It never mentioned his opponent, republican Barry Goldwater. The ad played on a fear voters already held, that Goldwater might start a nuclear war. Republicans protested loudly, Democrats pulled the spot, and the uproar got it rebroadcast in full on network news.

I study how emotional appeals persuade, from how viewers’ moods shape their reactions to political ads to how anxiety drives people to seek out, and sometimes fail to absorb, information about threats.
The LBJ “Daisy” ad shows why political campaigns to this day continue to reach for fear, and it hints at why the payoff is less predictable than you might think.
Fear is an alarm. It tells you something threatening is close. You feel scared when you believe you are at risk from something dangerous that can hurt you.
Anxiety knocks people off autopilot, sharpens attention and sends them looking for new information. That heightened attentiveness may be exactly what a struggling campaign wants.

When political scientists Travis Ridout and Kathleen Searles tracked Senate ads from 2004, they found that front-runners often leaned on enthusiasm and pride in their messaging, while candidates who were behind leaned on fear and anger.
Sometimes, fear works.

During the 1998 Massachusetts governor’s race, political scientist Ted Brader ran a study that embedded campaign ads in a news broadcast and changed only the music and images, keeping the words identical. Those changes produced completely different reactions. When a negative ad paired grainy black-and-white images of drug use with tense music, viewers paid closer attention to the spoken message and became more open to reconsidering their chosen candidate.

Fear cues – like a nuclear mushroom cloud – can push viewers to weigh fresh information and reconsider their choice. One surprise: Politically informed citizens were more responsive to these emotional cues than less engaged ones. Fear is not simply a tool for swaying the uninformed, undecided voter. It also reaches people who follow politics closely. Emotion provides the motivation, while knowledge provides the ability to think carefully about the issues and positions and seek out more information.

More broadly, a meta-analysis of over 100 studies found that fear appeals reliably shift attitudes and behavior across health and other domains. For instance, public health researcher Lucy Popova tested fear-based messages designed to discourage smokers from trying snus, a smokeless tobacco product. She found that when participants perceived a serious threat but also felt capable of acting on it, they held less favorable attitudes toward snus and were less inclined to try it.

Political attack ads – fear messaging being one type – have a shakier record. A review of more than 100 studies found no dependable evidence that negative campaigning wins elections, and some evidence that it lowers positive feelings toward the candidate who sponsors it.

Communication scholar Kim Witte’s research found that fear motivates action when people believe there is a workable response that they can carry out. When the threat feels big and the solution feels out of reach, people protect themselves from the message instead. They tune out, deny the threat or decide the messenger is the problem.

For example, picture an ad geared toward adolescent vaping that shows teens in hospital beds with ventilators using scary terms like “popcorn lungs.” If the ad also communicates that vaping can destroy lungs irreversibly, the teen audience is likely to experience extreme fear while at the same time feeling like there’s no way to fix the problem.

My colleagues and I have seen this effect in our own experiments. We found that people who felt highly anxious and also confident they could act sought out the most information. Those who felt anxious but lacked that confidence did go looking, yet they recalled very little. Anxiety pushed them to search but got in the way of absorbing what they read.
A campaign that frightens voters without offering a clear step to address the issue could end up producing plenty of anxious attention and very little learning.

Empowerment also helps explain who shows up at the polls. Political scientist Nicholas Valentino and colleagues found that anger boosted voter participation more reliably than anxiety, and anxiety mattered mainly for people who already had the skills and resources to take actions like donate to campaigns, attend rallies, sign petitions and so on.
Fear does its most reliable work when it attaches to a stereotype voters already carry. The 1988 presidential race provides two classic examples.

One controversial ad, produced in support of Republican George H.W. Bush, showed a mugshot of a Black man. The ad named the man, Willie Horton, and a voiceover explained that he’d committed rape and assault while on a weekend furlough from prison as part of a program run under Massachusetts Governor Michael Dukakis, the Democratic candidate. The spot linked fears about crime to race without saying so directly.

Bush’s campaign followed up with the “Revolving Door” ad, which built on that anxiety. It featured stark, black-and-white footage of inmates marching through a revolving gate while a narrator warned that Dukakis had let murderers out of prison on weekend passes.

Political scientist Tali Mendelberg’s research described in “The Race Card” shows that these implicit appeals to prejudices and fears are powerful. But they lose much of their force once someone publicly names them as racial. Implicit appeals work because they slip past most voters’ commitment to racial equality; once the racial message is pointed out, voters recognize it and many reject it rather than see themselves as endorsing prejudice.
Gender works in a similar way.

In a national experiment, Public Policy researcher Mirya Holman and colleagues found that when campaign messages triggered fears of terrorism, voters turned to their stereotypes of strong leaders as masculine. Those stereotypes hurt a female Democratic candidate, while Republican candidates of either gender were unaffected, since Republicans are already seen as tough on security.

A message communicating a threat does not need to name a candidate’s identity to disadvantage them. It simply makes voters reach for the stereotypes they already hold. There’s less systematic research on candidates’ religion, though the same mechanism – fear pushing voters to rely on the stereotypes they already hold about who can keep them safe – predicts similar vulnerability for Muslim candidates.

title: Why ultra-Orthodox parties hold so much sway in Israeli politics
paragraphs: On Oct. 20, 2026, a week before Israel’s elections, dozens of men were detained on suspicion of evading the draft – arrests that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called “unacceptable.”

The young men attend ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, religious schools, whose students were long exempt from the military service mandatory for most Israelis. A 2024 court ruling that Haredi men must be drafted alongside other Jewish youth intensified the conscription debate. Netanyahu’s government has failed to either legalize the draft exemption or enforce the court’s ruling, though he has said Haredim who are not studying should enlist.

With Israel’s military fighting in several conflicts, those exemptions have become increasingly unpopular: The vast majority of Jewish voters want Haredi communities to share the burden. Haredi political parties, however, are key potential coalition members as Netanyahu attempts to secure his political future. Although a relatively small percentage of the population, the Haredim hold disproportionate sway in Israel’s parliamentary system.

Haredi Jews strictly observe Jewish religious law and often disapprove of liberal interpretations. They typically live in Haredi-majority neighborhoods where large families are the norm – six children, on average – and about half of the men devote themselves to full-time religious study. The poverty rate is 33%, more than double the percentage for non-Haredi Jews.

The Israeli public is about 14% Haredi, but the community is growing quickly because of its high birth rate. Projections by the Central Bureau of Statistics estimate that almost a quarter of Israelis will be Haredi by 2050.

Haredi communities are diverse and represented by two main political parties. Haredim who are Ashkenazi – Jews whose ancestors came from northern and eastern Europe – are linked to United Torah Judaism, or UTJ. Those who are Sephardi or Mizrachi, meaning their ancestors came from the Iberian Peninsula and the Middle East, are linked to Shas.

A third Haredi party, Haredi Public, was formed in July 2026. The party says it will represent Haredim who feel underserved by Shas and UTJ, emphasizing employment and poverty, housing development and the education system. Unlike the other two Haredi parties, it has included women on its candidate list.

Elections for the Israeli parliament, the Knesset, use a proportional representation system. Any party that receives more than 3.25% of votes receives seats based on the fraction of votes it received. Each party allocates its seats to members based on a list of candidates published before elections.

Having multiple parties with similar target demographics risks dividing the vote, leaving that group with fewer representatives in the Knesset. Shas and UTJ have agreed to share their surplus votes in the 2026 election to maximize their overall seat share.

Because of the low electoral threshold, many parties are able to win seats. No Israeli party has ever attained the 50% share needed to control parliament by itself. As in other countries with similar systems, it is very common for parties to form coalitions and govern as a team.

Likud, one of the major conservative parties, has led most governing coalitions for the past two decades, with party leader Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister. Haredi parties are seen as strong conservative allies, and they have been key coalition members for Likud administrations. Today, as Netanyahu faces challenges from other right-wing parties over his handling of Oct. 7, 2023, and several wars, Likud may need them even more.
The fact that Likud has needed Haredi parties to form coalitions has given them negotiating power. For many years, one of their priorities has been draft exemptions for religious education.

Military service is mandatory for most groups in Israel, although Muslim and Christian Arab citizens are generally exempted. Jewish Israelis see conscription as a unifying experience and a costly demonstration of commitment to the state. Starting at age 18, most women serve two years and most men serve almost three years. Former soldiers can be called up as reservists into their 40s, depending on their training.

For decades, Haredi men received de facto exemptions. It was, effectively, one of several government arrangements that subsidize Haredi communities. Religious schools for teen boys and married men receive government payments for each student. Given the communities’ low employment rates, large families and high poverty rates, many families rely on public support.

In 2024, Israel’s Supreme Court ruled that a blanket exemption from military service for Haredim was not legal. Netanyahu’s government struggled to enact a compromise between those who favored drafting Haredim and the Haredi parties; the failure to find a lasting legal way to exempt Haredi men led Shas and UTJ to leave the Likud-led coalition in 2025.
Nonetheless, this ruling has not led to mass conscription.

Haredi groups have held public protests, and many have ignored draft notices. While tens of thousands of men are draft eligible but not serving, and most of them are Haredi, fewer than 500 evaders have been arrested in 2026. Netanyahu argues against arrests, saying they discourage men from enlisting without coercion.

In July 2026, at the urging of Haredi parties, the government passed a law to temporarily prevent arresting draft evaders. Some members of Netanyahu’s governing coalition opposed the law, however, and right-wing opposition parties filed petitions to challenge it in court.

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett – leader of the Together alliance, and seen as a key contender to oust Netanyahu – has threatened to cut subsidies to the Haredi community if they continue to defy the draft. Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the centrist Yashar party, is another top contender to replace Netanyahu. He has proposed allowing 3% of Haredi men exemptions to study, while drafting the majority.

As the number of conflict zones increases – Gaza, southern Lebanon and Iran, as well as deployments in the West Bank – the unequal burden of military participation is a growing source of resentment among many conscripted Israelis and their families. Seven in 10 Jewish Israelis favor drafting the Haredim.
Shas and UTJ, however, have declared they will not join a coalition unless it promises to codify the draft exemption into law.

When the Haredi parties exited Netanyahu’s coalition, Likud replaced them with nationalist parties that emphasize the state and Jewish supremacy. Particularly notable was the decision to include the Jewish Power party, an offshoot of an earlier group banned for racism; including Kahanist groups was long seen as a red line.

Haredi communities, on the other hand, tend to prioritize religious Jewishness over the state. Most Haredim do not consider themselves Zionist, and a small percentage are anti-Zionist. They argue that it was sacrilegious for people to create a state of Israel rather than waiting for God to return Jews to the land of Israel. Where nationalist politicians emphasize the secular state and military service, Haredim see their religious study as service to the Jewish community.

As Likud’s changing coalition shows, Netanyahu’s alliances are strategic rather than ideological. I believe his decision to side with the Haredim on the recent draft legislation suggests his coalition is open to revision after the October 2026 election.

title: PHP is in the foundation of 70% of websites – here’s what it is and why a flaw in the software is a major hacking threat
paragraphs: Governments and organizations around the world began scrambling on Oct. 21, 2026, to fix a vulnerability in software that runs their websites, a bug that could give hackers access to data and control of websites. The flaw in PHP, the programming language that powers much of today’s web, prompted urgent warnings from the U.S. National Security Agency, cybersecurity agencies and software vendors.

A researcher at Calif, a security research firm, found the flaw in August 2026 using an advanced artificial intelligence model from OpenAI. The firm alerted the nonprofit that manages PHP. However, word of the flaw leaked before the PHP organization released patches for its software, and according to Amazon Web Services officials, hackers began “broadly” attempting to exploit it.

The vulnerability has implications far beyond a single company or platform, because PHP is a key piece of software that helps run millions of websites. So, what is PHP, what role did AI play in uncovering the vulnerability, and should the average user worry?

PHP is a programming language that powers most websites. For a modern website to provide dynamic content, visual elements and searchable features, a program must run on the web server and take user input, whether that is entering a web address or clicking links and buttons. Estimates suggest that around 70% of websites run on PHP.

PHP operates on a web server in two main parts: the core PHP system – the engine and runtime libraries – and the individual PHP scripts, which are the custom programs that actually implement a website. When you interact with a website, PHP scripts run, take user input and produce the output your web browser displays.

The current security issue sits directly in the core PHP system and the libraries it uses. When a vulnerability exists at this deep level, it can allow an adversary to exploit the system. In this case, they can run unauthorized commands on the computer hosting the website, which allows attackers to access data and gain full control of the website.

This vulnerability is not a mistake in an individual website’s code. The issue lies in the core PHP system, making every unpatched system running PHP vulnerable. Since websites are accessible to anyone on the internet, adversaries can easily find PHP-based websites using automated tools. From there, they can run an exploit program that takes advantage of the vulnerability.

This exploit code is called PHP2Shell. This name comes from the fact that the exploit gives the attacker “shell access,” a cybersecurity term for direct command-line control of the computer running the website. Shell access bypasses the website interface, giving adversaries a window to enter commands and access all the website’s data.

What makes this vulnerability particularly interesting is how it was discovered. This exploit came to light through a process known as coordinated disclosure, in which cybersecurity researchers report the flaw to PHP developers before publicizing it.

This discovery shows the power of AI in cybersecurity. For decades, finding subtle software flaws required large teams of specialists manually reviewing code. Today’s AI systems can examine vast codebases and identify unusual patterns in hours or days. These models can analyze millions of lines of code in seconds, spotting subtle memory management bugs that human auditors might miss over decades of software development. The PHP vulnerability has existed in the core PHP code for over a decade, and AI helped researchers find it.

However, this also shows that attackers can use these same tools to locate and exploit vulnerabilities. The same reasoning capabilities that help security researchers find flaws first can also let attackers rapidly scan the web for vulnerable targets and automate the creation of tools to exploit the vulnerabilities.
This illustrates why it is so critical for security teams to use AI to find vulnerabilities and report them safely and actively. AI can also help release patches that mitigate these vulnerabilities.

Many government agencies, universities, hospitals and businesses rely on PHP-based systems. While individual internet users are unlikely to be directly affected, organizations that delay patching could expose sensitive data, risk having their operations disrupted or give attackers a foothold into larger networks.
PHP runs entirely on remote web servers. If you are an everyday internet user visiting websites, you do not need to download a patch or fix your personal computer.

However, if you manage a website, blog or server, even a small site built on popular content management systems such as WordPress, you should check your server administration panel or web host immediately to ensure your PHP software is updated to the latest patched version. If a third party hosts your website, check with them to see whether they have patched for these vulnerabilities.

The PHP2Shell discovery illustrates a new reality for cybersecurity. In our interconnected world, keeping web infrastructure secure is a continuous race. As AI tools become standard for both cyber defenders and online adversaries, maintaining fast patching habits remains our most essential defense.

title: UN peacekeepers prepare to exit Lebanon after 70 years – leaving behind a worrying security vacuum
paragraphs: For nearly 70 years, the blue helmets of United Nations’ peacekeepers have dotted the landscape of southern Lebanon. But those days may soon be over.
Under Israeli and American pressure, the U.N. Security Council unanimously voted in August to end the mandate establishing the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, or UNIFIL.
It means the 7,565 members of UNIFIL deployed in Lebanon – representing about 46 countries – will depart the country no later than Dec. 31, 2026.

The end of the U.N. presence comes at a pivotal time. Israel and Lebanon have already held seven rounds of negotiations aimed at bringing a lasting peace to a region that has suffered from decades of conflict.

Brokered by the United States, these talks that led to the signing of the Trilateral Framework in June 2026 call for the disarmament of Hezbollah, the Israeli withdrawal from all Lebanese lands and the settlement of all disputes over borders. Yet all of these conditions are still some way off from completion – and beset by a series of barriers.

As such, the departure of the United Nations peacekeeping forces raises serious concerns. The potential for a security vacuum looms large in south Lebanon, especially given that Israel continues to bomb Lebanon despite a ceasefire that has nominally been in place since April 16, 2026.

As a scholar of Middle East Studies, I know that UNIFIL has never been a permanent solution. But I fear that its termination creates more problems than it solves, especially when there are no clear replacements or post-UNIFIL security arrangements in place.
While the U.N. had had an on-the-ground presence in Lebanon to handle civil strife since the 1950s, its role in mediating between Lebanon and Israel started later.

In 1978, after a series of attacks on Israel organized by Palestinian fighters in Lebanon, Israel invaded and occupied the south in what was known as Operation Litani. As a result, the United Nations Security Council established UNIFIL to monitor Israel’s withdrawal from south Lebanon and to restore peace at the Lebanese–Israeli border.

Israel’s occupation of south Lebanon lasted more than two decades. Following its withdrawal on May 25, 2000, the U.N. set the Blue Line – a 75-mile (120 km) demarcation line created for the practical purpose of confirming Israeli withdrawal from south Lebanon. It was not an official border but a buffer zone monitored by the U.N. peacekeepers.
UNFIL and the Blue Line served as geographic and diplomatic focal points in the 2006 war between Hezbollah – an Iranian-backed militia operating from Lebanon – and Israel.

Resolution 1701 of the Security Council, which brought an end to the 2006 war, dramatically expanded the UNIFIL role in Lebanon; the number of troops went from 2,000 to 15,000 authorized military personnel.

Its mandate also changed to include monitoring the ceasefire and documenting its violations, coordinating with Lebanon’s military and functioning as the only direct communication channel between the Lebanese and Israeli militaries. UNIFIL also offered humanitarian aid to the affected civilian population of south Lebanon.

Yet UNIFIL’s role never altered the basic lack of peace on the Israeli-Lebanese border. Over 50 years, Israel invaded Lebanon numerous times. And since 2000, Hezbollah has flourished in south Lebanon.

As UNIFIL prepares to depart, it’s unclear what will fill the looming security vacuum. It could be filled by non-U.N. troops, but Lebanon’s past shows the risks inherent to international peacekeeping missions.

In 1982, after Israel invaded Lebanon and occupied Beirut with the intention of eliminating the Palestinian militant threat, Lebanese authorities called on Western powers for help. In August, the governments of the U.S., France, Italy and the United Kingdom created a multinational peacekeeping force designed to restore peace and stop the fighting between the Lebanese, Palestinians and Israelis.
But on Oct. 23, 1983, the multinational peacekeeping force was the target of a dual suicide attack that killed 241 American service members and 58 French paratroopers.
To this day, the attack – claimed by the pro-Iranian Islamic Jihad – remains the deadliest single-day incident for the U.S. Marine Corps since the Battle of Iwo Jima in 1945.
In addition to Israel, interventions in Lebanon have also come from another neighboring country.

In 1976, the Syrian military intervened during Lebanon’s civil war to put an end to sectarian violence. Nearly three decades of occupation followed, and troops were withdrawn only following the assassination of Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri in 2005 and the subsequent Cedar Revolution.
With the absence of an internal Lebanese consensus, the arrival of any international peacekeeping force to replace the exiting UNIFIL will be perceived by many Lebanese as a top-down imposition.

Moreover, the situation on the ground makes it dangerous for any international force to successfully operate. Israel is reportedly occupying over 10% of Lebanon’s territories, including multiple permanent bases and outposts in southern Lebanese territory.
Hezbollah, meanwhile, refuses to disarm.
Finally, the fate of Lebanon-Israel direct negotiations is unclear. Recently, the countries held military talks in Florida, but little is expected from them.

title: Ancestors all around – millions of dead people linger in Americans’ memories
paragraphs: Halloween kicks off a series of religious and cultural festivals to honor the dead, including All Saints’ Day, All Souls’ Day and the Day of the Dead. But deceased loved ones don’t disappear from people’s social worlds once the ghost and skeleton decorations come down.

Present in memory and tradition, the dead can shape people’s identities and behaviors long after they die. Recent survey data shows that almost 44% of Americans report that they have felt the presence of a deceased relative or that they have communicated with a deceased relative in the past year alone.

Researchers lack basic knowledge about this shadow population. As demographers, we typically study the living. But in our recent work, we asked a very unusual demographic question: What does a population of our deceased relatives look like?

Our research typically categorizes the living population by age groups and other demographic attributes. In our recent study, we took our analysis a step further to estimate the size and age distribution of the currently living population’s deceased relatives. We focused specifically on deceased grandparents, parents, siblings, spouses and children.

To do this project, we relied on a modeling framework called demographic microsimulations. This approach produces results only for Black and white Americans. The method cannot estimate relative populations living outside of the United States, so it excludes groups with high percentages of foreign-born individuals who have family abroad.
Our study focused on the populations as of July 2020, but for the purposes of this article, we updated our analysis and weighted results to the estimated population as of October 2026.

Because estimating the deceased relative population is not a common exercise in our field, we had to make some modeling decisions. We counted only deceased relatives who died after the birth of at least one person still alive; if no one remains who could remember them, we did not include them.

Also, we counted deceased persons based on how many relatives they have in the living population. For example, if a deceased 60-year-old man is survived by a spouse, an adult child, a grandchild and a sibling, we count him in the deceased relative population four times, reflecting his being remembered by four living individuals. As such, the deceased relative population we quantified is really a count of how many direct relative ties remain to those who are dead.

And finally, we classified deceased relatives according to their age at death. We believe this represents the age many people will most clearly remember their deceased loved ones. Of course, we categorize the living population by their current age.
Our results included several key findings.

First, the deceased relative population is large. Our model estimated that the living Black and white populat,ion representing about 217 million people, had 755 million ties to deceased close relatives. That’s a population more than three times the size of the living population. For every under-15-year-old out trick-or-treating on Halloween, there are about 21 deceased relatives remembered.

Second, our model shows that, on average, the deceased relatives died 25 years ago. That the average deceased relative has been remembered for a quarter of a century makes it clear that loved ones are often suspended in memory for years, even decades, after their deaths.

Third, over half of the deceased relative population was born more than 100 years ago – even before the term “trick-or-treating” took hold in the U.S. Around 10% of the deceased relatives were born before 1900, with 140,000 of them born before the Civil War – these are the remembered grandparents of today’s oldest individuals. These results speak to how generations of the seemingly long ago past still have a direct tie to the living.

The Halloween season reminds us of ghosts, spirits and ancestors. Whatever their beliefs, many Americans also carry relationships with people who are no longer alive: grandparents whose recipes they still make, parents whose advice they still hear, spouses whose absence shapes their days.

These relationships are deeply personal, but together they form a vast and previously unstudied shadow population. By quantifying and characterizing the deceased relative population, our research reveals just how many people no longer appear in the census yet remain an integral part of our social world.
